speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that the former minister of fisheries had initiated a major policy review, leading to a white paper on fisheries development for the 1980s, and since that review would have included a reference to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry on the subject of fisheries licensing policies, including proposals contained in the Sinclair and Levelton reports, and whereas the standing committee should travel across Canada to hear first hand the views of fishermen, processors and others concerned with the fishery, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass):
That this House direct the government to make a reference to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry to conduct a thorough review of federal fisheries licensing policy, which would include travelling to the regions of Canada to hear first-hand the views of fishermen.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 43. Interest charges to business, particularly to small business, have caused and are causing extreme problems, despite the recent reduction of the prime rate. A number of businesses have had to seriously curtail their activities and cut back on employment because they are not able to finance receivables and inventories at current bank rates.
The minister has accepted the proposal made in the Crosbie budget to provide for small business development bonds. The minister presented some details of this proposal in his masquerade budget of April 21. Nearly three weeks have passed and no legislation has been introduced. No arrangements for debate of legislation have been made.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Since the initial price of top grade wheat has been established at $3.75 per bushel, which is 50 cents a bushel less than grain producers are now receiving and is far below the cost of production, since the lowering of North American export prices can be directly related to the U.S. embargo, and since the Prime Minister has assured us that this government will protect the grain producers from the effects of that embargo, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse):
That this government establish the initial price of top grade wheat at $4.25 per bushel, the present level being paid to grain producers.

In view of the fact that the government plan of reducing utility income tax rebate will create a situation where citizens of our country are not treated with equality, descriminating between farmers in each province so that, for example, the farmers in Alberta will be subjected to an extra cost for utilities from $100 to $200 per annum, as opposed to their counterparts in the province of Saskatchewan who will suffer no extra charge, I move, seconded by the hon. member from Pembina (Mr. Elzinga):

speechtext:

In light of the Fisheries Council of Canada's recent criticisms of the over-the-side sales agreement with Joint Trawlers Ltd., as well as the complete dissatisfaction of the provincial fisheries ministers of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island with the federal government's lack of meaningful consultation with them-and that is even more important-can the minister tell this House why he has elected to depart from the clearly-defined policy of his predecessor regarding over-the-side sales?

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subsubtopic: POLICY RESPECTING OVER-THE-SIDE SALES AGREEMENT WITH JOINT TRAWLERS LTD.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would leave it to the former minister, who is perfectly able to explain his own position, to see if he accepts the entire content of the hon. member's question.
Certainly, my predecessor had not prohibited over-the-side sales, but he did introduce conditions. One of the conditions was varied by me, as I felt that the situation of a guarantee being totally rejected would leave the fishermen in a position with very little bargaining power. A judgment call had to be made. Fish caught by Canadian fishermen will be made available in very small quantity, about 1 per cent of the total landing and 0.7 per cent of the total value, which means that the processors have control of some 99 per cent of the Canadian fish landings.
As far as the eastern fishermen's group was concerned, the application which they presented jointly with the processors contained the sort of loopholes which no government could accept. For example, at the end of each day a decision would be made on whether or not freezing capacity was required. I know of no freezer from overseas that can get to this side of the ocean on a day's notice.
With regard to the rest of the hon. member's question, provincial ministers have taken positions of this issue which are at some variance with the apparently united front which seems to have developed this week. Certainly, when I asked one of the privincial ministers in an important fishing province recently if he was against all over-the-side sales, he said that he still supported some such sales under good conditions.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

Madam Speaker, 1 would like to refer to two questions to which I have been referring for about three years approximately, perhaps longer. They have been repeated on successive order papers. I understand that the previous government was about to answer them in a much more timely fashion before it left office than the present government, which has taken two to three years to answer some questions. 1 refer specifically to question No. 15, which concerns a gentleman named Mr. Martin Goldfarb, Goldfarb Consultants Limited and the amount of public funds they have received for doing business for the present government and for the former Liberal government when it was in office.
I do not think it should take three years to figure out just what Martin Goldfarb has been getting in the way of payments for his services to the Liberal party as well as for his services to the government of this country. In other words, I think it is about time that these questions were answered. Three years is a long time. I have every right to complain vigorously about it because if it were three weeks, three months or four months, one could say that it takes a long time to compile statistical information, but it should not take three years. Three years means that something is being hidden.
My other question-the number of which 1 do not have readily available without having to flip through the order paper, but I am sure that the parliamentary secretary is well aware of it from its substance-is a question which has also been on successive order papers for a number of years. It involves the fingerprinting of civil servants by this government, both when it was in power previously and now. My question asks how many of them are there, why they were fingerprinted and so on. I am referring to public servants who are not in security positions, not connected with national security or national defence. I am referring to such people as secretaries and unemployment insurance officers who, I know, have in the past been frequently fingerprinted all across this country.
In my opinion, this is an invasion of privacy. Parliament has the right to know why this has been done. For three years I have been asking this question. I have raised at least five or six points of order, and for three years the government have been
sitting on their behinds, which seems to be what they usually do, and have not attempted to answer either of these questions.
Could the parliamentary secretary give us some indication right now-not tomorrow, not the next day, but right now- when these questions are going to be answered?

Madam Speaker, I welcome the intervention of the hon. member for Leeds-Grenville (Mr. Cossitt), and I should like to point out, as I did on Friday, that the present government has an admirable record in answering these questions when one compares it with the record of the former government in the Thirty-first Parliament. I would ask the hon. member to look at my answer given in reply to the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton last Friday on the rapidity with which questions are answered in this House.
My role is merely to report to the House those questions which are answered by departments. It is not for me as Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council to comment any further on these questions. I suggest that if the hon. member is not satisfied with a particular answer, he can take it up in the usual way. He can ask questions in the House, he can ask further questions on the order paper, he can avail himself of the "late show". There are a number of things he could do in addition to resorting to private correspondence with ministers.
He brought up a couple of specific questions. One is question No. 15 with respect to Mr. Goldfarb. I will try to get the answer for him as quickly as possible, but it is my recollection that since the session started we have answered a number of questions from the hon. member. I think he is doing very well in comparison with other members in the House. Mind you, I should say that the hon. member for Leeds-Grenville is one of the few members of the House who has practically filled up the order paper with questions, so he cannot expect answers to all his questions immediately.
With regard to the question concerning fingerprinting-I forget the number-he asserts that the answer was ready to be given by the former government. I ask him to consult with his leader and the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton, who was president of the privy council at that time, to ascertain why, if these questions have indeed gone through the departments, they were not tabled in the House. But I will try to expedite all the questions in the course of my normal duties.

Madam Speaker, I do not want to prolong this debate but I cannot fail to make two observations about the remarks of the parliamentary secretary.
As I understand the role of the parliamentary secretary, he does not stand up in the House and spout answers which are given to him by various ministries in response to different questions. The hon. member for Leeds-Grenville has asked that a question which has been on the order paper for three years in successive Parliaments be answered. I think there is a duty in those circumstances on the part of the parliamentary secretary to answer those questions if he can. If he cannot, I think it is inappropriate for him not to say that he will use his best efforts, as Parliamentary Secretary to President of the
May 8, 1980

Privy Council responsible for the operation of the Elouse, to obtain answers for the hon. member for Leeds-Grenville and indeed for any other member of the House of Commons.
I will not argue the statistical record because I think it is a very foolish argument and we can deal with statistics any way we like. We are talking about the principle of the government answering questions put by members.
If there is some reason respecting the security of the country for the question not to be answered, then the hon. member is entitled to know. If the reason is that it is an embarrassing question for the government, then I think that is not sufficient reason to fail to answer the question. Certainly that question would not have been an embarrassing matter to the government of the right hon. member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), who is now Leader of the Opposition. But apparently it is embarrassing or something to the present government because it has not been answered by the parliamentary secretary or former parliamentary secretaries. The question is now for the third time on the order paper.
All I am saying to my friend is that he has the duty, not just to give us the statistics, but to say to members, when questions are persistently left unanswered, what they can do to obtain the answers or at least to inform the hon. member why the question cannot be answered. I think it is extremely important that we establish that at the beginning because I think it is important to the relationship which exists between the government and the opposition in terms of the operation of the House of Commons and House business.
1 put it to my friend very seriously that three years is a long time to wait for any answer. The hon. member for Leeds-Grenville indicated the position on a prior occasion when we had the privilege of forming the Government of Canada. He said that the answers were ready, that they were to come on, but that they did not come on because of the fall of the government. If those answers were ready for our government, those answers are now ready for his government. I suggest he go to see the Clerk of the Privy Council immediately, obtain those answers, if they are ready as he says they are, and bring them forward to the House. I think it will simplify matters, and certainly it will be helpful in terms of the flow of information to which I believe members of Parliament are entitled.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO FORMULATE HONEST AND EFFECTIVE ENERGY POLICY
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to formulate an honest and effective energy policy.
He said: Mr. Speaker will note that we as the official opposition have chosen to use this our first allotted day to bring to the attention of the House and to our fellow citizens the failure of this government to deal honestly and effectively with a variety of important and urgent problems in the field of national energy policy.
Some of the problems which will be discussed today are as follows: first, pricing and supply; second, consumer impact; third, conservation and alternative sources; fourth, economic and industrial impact. I think it will be obvious to the House in terms of both importance and urgency that any one of these several issues alone could form the subject matter of today's debate. In terms of the total energy situation, I should like to point out that this list obviously is not an exhaustive one.
Any opposition acting responsibly could be justified in devoting allotted days to a variety of other energy-related issues. For example, one thinks immediately of the fact that Canadians are entitled to know, and we are entitled to debate, the international aspects of energy, particularly those aspects which gave rise to what we know around the world in this era as the energy crisis. Similarly, it would take little to justify using an allotted day to debate the energy dimension of Canada-United States relations.
Of course, there are numerous other energy issues which demand and deserve our attention. However, we feel compelled to bring to the attention of the House the four matters I have enumerated because it is our view that to ignore any one of those would, as an official opposition, be irresponsible. That irresponsibility would not be less than the irresponsibility of


May 8, 1980
Energy Policy
the government in failing to deal effectively with all four of those issues. Perhaps the combining of all four of those issues enumerated in this debate will serve at least to emphasize their interrelationship and their interdependence, because among the multitude of sins committed by this government in the energy field-and by previous Liberal governments-has been the sin of ignoring or failing to comprehend this interdependence.
The only more serious charge that I could lay at the doorstep of this government and previous Liberal governments would be their guilt in forsaking any medium or long-term energy strategy for the sake of short-term political expedience. We have had years of announcements by a parade of ministers of finance and ministers of energy. I recall at least two ministers of finance in the last few years talking endlessly about the necessity of moving toward, to or beyond world prices in oil. We have had at least two ministers of energy announcing a conservation strategy which they thought was so good that they reannounced it several times in several sessions. Of course, it was never fully and certainly never effectively implemented, because it faced that one insurmountable hurdle-the hurdle of Liberal political expediency.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO FORMULATE HONEST AND EFFECTIVE ENERGY POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO FORMULATE HONEST AND EFFECTIVE ENERGY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker will hear one of my colleagues, the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), dealing with energy pricing and supply. We in this party find it unacceptable that this government's attention span to self-sufficiency lasts no longer than one month following the latest Middle East crisis. That is the entire attention span of this government. Following that one month it is completely ignored.
In our view, this government takes greater satisfaction in concluding deals with foreign suppliers of oil than seizing upon the challenges and the opportunity to become self-sufficient from our own resources. We do not believe that enormous payments of Canadian dollars from Canadian taxpayers to foreign producers need be the destiny of our country. It takes little imagination for anyone in this House of whatever political persuasion to realize what we could be doing with the $3 billion we are paying out today in subsidy payments alone. Think of it if you wish, sir, in economic or industrial or regional development terms. Others may choose to think of it in terms of the enhancement of social programs. Others may think of it in terms of the reduction of the national debt. But if Mr. Speaker wishes to think of it purely in energy terms, I point out that that $3 billion would provide $500 worth of new insulation in virtually every home in Canada. In turning its back on self-sufficiency, this government is committed to the continuation of this enormous and endless drain for an indefinite period.
In terms of pricing, sir, when the government talks about pricing it talks exclusively about price at the pump. Sometimes, rather rarely, it talks in terms of prices in regard to revenue sharing between producing and non-producing provinces. But never does this government talk about price in the most important context-in terms of bringing on required Canadian production.
Does this government ever ask itself, for example, at what price is tertiary development from conventional sources viable?
I suggest it never does. Does it ever ask itself at what price is Alsands viable, given the enormous capital investment, or at what price is gasohol, solar or tidal energy practical? I suggest never.
Pricing to this government is first a matter of algebra; it is the xyz formula, the nature of which has been and continues to be a secret. Second, when it talks about price it talks about taxes, whether they be refinery taxes, export taxes consumer taxes, next year's taxes or the taxes for the year after, all of which remain secret.
Perhaps it was put best by The Globe and Mail, coincidentally just this morning, in its editorial. It states:
It is useless to complain that the government is trying to find ways of replacing the excise tax which it said it would not levy. The government has done little but evade its election promises since the election. Why expect honour?
Another of my colleagues will be dealing with the impact upon Canadian consumers. Indeed, that is not a problem that is confined to the gas pumps, as this government would have us believe. Any Canadian consumer is entitled to ask, what is the future of low-income groups who must heat their homes? What about those on fixed incomes, what is their future, particularly senior citizens who, possibly to the surprise of this government, do not drive large gas-guzzling cars to the pumps?
What about the enormous disparity that already exists among Canadians-and one thinks immediately of those in Quebec and Atlantic Canada-as compared to those in other parts of the country? How much greater is this disparity to be allowed to grow? Is there to be any form of energy cost cushion? Will there be an energy tax credit? Is there to be a subsidization of the generation of electricity in Atlantic Canada? Apparently that is not to be, Mr. Speaker. Therefore, many of those Canadians least able to protect themselves will become even more vulnerable in the future should this government's policies continue to develop as they have over the past few months.
The third point we will be raising, sir, will be in respect of conservation and alternative sources. I confess that I am not convinced this government has made that one basic decision yet, and that decision is, do we implement conservation measures or do we ration gasoline? 1 do not believe that decision has been made. There is no indication that it has.
Hon. members will remember former energy minister Donald Macdonald announcing a conservation measure in February, 1975. It was reannounced by his successor, the Hon. Alastair Gillespie, in 1976. What has been implemented? I suggest virtually nothing. The conclusion one reaches is that this government, as previous Liberal governments, is content with a 3.5 per cent increase in energy consumption. That is the inescapable conclusion one must draw, even in the face of not just independent studies, but its own government studies which

May 8, 1980

say that 2 per cent is attainable. What is the government's response? All we have seen so far has been the throne speech. We have an awesome conservation program consisting entirely of two things; fuel efficient standards for cars, and higher home insulation standards. That is the total conservation package we have had from this government.
What then, sir, has the government said or done about alternative sources? Again one looks to the throne speech, and 1 quote:
An alternative energy corporation will be created with a mandate to stimulate the development of new and renewable energy sources to replace oil.
The sole response to the challenge, the opportunity of developing alternatives, is another Crown corporation. Today in a reply to a question from one of his colleagues, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) said this corporation will become a subsidiary of PetroCan, that it will have a board of directors and, I think, $20 million capitalization. He was not asked where the head office was to be, but I presume it is Calgary, a marvellous city in which to live. 1 am envious of those defeated Liberal candidates who can catch on to this Crown corporation, and there are lots of them out in Alberta. The only reason, frankly, that I see for putting this subsidiary in Calgary, much as I like the city, is its proximity to defeated Liberal candidates.
Where does this failure to respond to this challenge leave a variety of projects? Where, for example, does this leave the potential in Ontario for gasohol and alternative liquid fuels as dealt with in the Ontario budget? Where does this leave the tidal power project on the Annapolis River? Where does it leave the biomass project in Prince Edward Island? What about the Donkin No. 2 coal project in Nova Scotia? And the list goes on and on. Those projects remain at the mercy of our 432nd Crown corporation. I confess I am not sure about the numbers, but it is four hundred and something, and I believe it is 432. It is close to the 500 mark.
These projects are at the mercy of this newest Crown corporation, to be a subsidiary of PetroCan, located in Calgary, with a yet unnamed board of directors. These important projects, as you will recall, Mr. Speaker, were some of those to flow from our proposed national energy bank. Others, you will recall, included Canadian-owned oil upgraders, because we are exporting oil we do not have the capacity to deal with it at this time. That was another project. Then there was the oil sands project and the gas pipeline to Quebec City and through to the maritimes. Then we had proposals for urban transit, which we heard yesterday were now being discarded. We had urban transit upon which Liberal candidates have run for almost half a century, I believe. Are all of these projects-I say this more in sadness than in anger-and our ability to harness the alternatives with which we are so rich to have the same fate as urban transit? Is that the energy future for Canada and for Canadians?

The second comment I would like to make is that I understand that the minister of energy in Alberta, Mr. Leitch, today introduced a bill which would allow Alberta to curtail production in the oil fields "in the public interest". It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that it is not in the public interest, or of the rest of Canada at least, for us to have a confrontation in this country between "two gun slingers meeting in the Alberta corral to shoot it out" in order to get an oil deal. I happen to agree with that decision. Indeed, it was suggested many years ago with a little bit of foresight by Tommy Douglas in this House that that pricing deal was wrong. I agree with what the minister said but I do not agree with the way he did it. I think it was an opening shot, so we now find Mr. Leitch and Mr. Lougheed taking their turn at bluffing. I am a western member and 1 have a lot of sympathy for some of the views of the province of Alberta. If there were ever a time for politicians in Canada, whether it be the minister of energy sitting over there or the premiers of

1 would like to take the time to deal with some of the remarks made by the Conservative spokesman, the hon. member for Perth. I should tell him that the New Democratic Party rejected the Conservative government's energy policy, as did the Canadian people. There were very good reasons for rejecting that policy. One of the main reasons we rejected it was because of the split-up of the wealth after that excise tax was to be applied. What was to happen to that money which was to have been taken out of the pockets of the Canadian consumers? Where was it to go? Well, $33 billion was to go to the industry, $40 billion to Alberta and only $17 billion to the federal government. And not all of that $17 billion was earmarked for energy programs; some of it was going to be put into the mortgage interest deductibility scheme, which was really a subsidy for upper middle-income people.
We approved of some of the measures in that budget, the energy tax credit and so on. We spoke favourably about some of them. But generally it was a lousy policy which redistributed wealth into the hands of the people who did not need it, namely the oil companies, and also into the hands of one single province. We rejected that and so did the Canadian people.
While the minister was talking about Petro-Canada, I heard some Conservative backbenchers call it a "peanut operation". We in the New Democratic Party do not believe that it should be or is a peanut operation. The Conservative party had four policies on Petro-Canada. All of them were intended to privatize Petro-Canada. The Canadian people did not approve of that and they made their views known in the election. Where 1 come from it was an important issue in the election campaign.
The Conservatives have proposed the following resolution:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to formulate an honest and effective energy policy.
We agree with that resolution, but it is much like the pot calling the kettle black when the Conservatives propose it. Since that time there has been a variety of interpretation as to whether you were talking about specifically the $4.00, the $4.50/54.50 formula, or whether you were talking about keeping the increases below a less defined but possibly higher price related to world levels. Could you tell us now whether or not you are committed to keeping the price increases below $4.50 a barrel for the next three years or whether you are talking about something else?
The Prime Minister answered the following:
I was talking in the terms which you just quoted, and I did not ask myself the question you are asking now: Would that mean much lower in one year and slightly lower in other years or much lower in average over the whole period? I think you can read it the way you want-
Q. Then you are saying that there is no commitment to keep the increases below $4.50 a barrel in the following three years?
A. Well, in each of the three years?
Q. Yes.
A. Well, I have just answered. You can take it in whatever way you want, so can Mr. Lougheed, Mr. Blakeney and Mr. Lalonde.
The minister is sitting over there.
The important thing is that we get a better deal for Canadians in pricing over those four years . . . You shake your head. 1 will take supplementaries on this if you want.
The pressman said "no". There were no supplementaries.
1 used to know an Indian chief in Alberta who used to say that sometimes when white men talk they speak in gob-bledygook. Surely this is an example of gobbledygook, of trying to weasel around a campaign promise. The Prime Minister is very prone to speak philosophically in this House. Through the minister I ask him what the cost, in terms of political morality, of this promise is.

-what any village graybeard in the Ukraine or Russia had understood from time immemorial and could have explained to the progressive commentators ages ago, had the commentators ever found the time in that dizzy fever of theirs to consult him: that a dozen worms can't go on and on gnawing the same apple forever, that if the earth is a finite object, then its expanses and resources are finite also, and the endless, infinite progress dinned into our heads by the dreamers of the Enlightenment cannot be accomplished on it.

Can we change direction? 1 think that upon the answer to that question depends the future of the world we know, of our environment and of our country.

Also I suggest that if the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) re-examines what the Premier of Saskatchewan has been saying about oil pricing and revenues, he would be less quick to insist that the New Democratic Party is united. The Premier of Saskatchewan is every bit as vigorous although much more skilful at hiding than the Premier of Alberta.
I should like to commence my remarks with a quotation from a newspaper article which appeared on May 1 in the Calgary Herald. It reads as follows:
Lack of credibility at the political level is costing this country dearly according to the president of the C.D. Howe Institute. Carl Beigie told a Calgary Chamber of Commerce luncheon on Wednesday that the world will survive the Iranian crisis and Canada will survive the Quebec referendum. But, he said, Canada won't survive for long under the current "deterioration of government credibility". The prime example of this breakdown, he said, is Ottawa's energy pricing policy.
That statement was not made by a Progressive Conservative partisan. It was not made by an oil company executive. It was not made by an Alberta politician or even a resident of Alberta or western Canada. That statement was made by a resident of Montreal, the president of the non-partisan, Montreal-based C.D. Howe Research Institute. He said that the biggest threat to Canada is not the Quebec referendum but this government, particularly this government's energy-pricing policy.

speechtext: He is an American.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO FORMULATE HONEST AND EFFECTIVE ENERGY POLICY
speechtext:
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), who did not have the courtesy to hang around, proved what we had to say about honesty in that fatuous and false excuse he gave for leaving. He started his remarks by saying that we have nerve to raise this issue, that this party has nerve to raise this issue. I would suggest that he has colossal gall to sit there and suggest that what they have been doing and saying is anything else but totally destructive to the country, as evidenced by a research institute in his own backyard. In the view of the C.D. Howe Institute, this government's energy pricing policy is simply incredible, lacking any credibility whatsoever. Also, it is totally dishonest.
A friend of mine who happened to be in Germany shortly after the recent election, told me about an editorial which he read in a German newspaper. It described Canada's reaction to the 18-cent a gallon excise tax as resembling that of a central American banana republic. In other words, to Europeans the energy-pricing policies as articulated by the Liberal party are the subject of ridicule, equivalent to those that one would expect of a banana republic. Yet we have this government apparently feeling proud to be compared with a banana republic.
In the Speech from the Throne, in the mini-budget and repeatedly in the House, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources stated that the one decision they have taken is that they will not increase the excise tax by 18 cents a gallon this year, as if somehow this negative decision required some great act of courage and would be so helpful to this nation. Somehow behaving like a central American
banana republic is a marvellous thing to this group, however embarrassing it is for the rest of the world to view us as a banana republic because of the positions taken by the Liberal government, the tired old Liberal government.
The most serious criticism that could be made is the fundamental dishonesty of what the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources have been saying. They claimed repeatedly and erroneously that they are saving the consumers of Canada billions of dollars. What consumers are they talking about? What are they really saying? Are they really saving consumers anything?
Consistent with their dishonest approach, the government failed to recognize that the budget of December 11 provided an energy tax credit for those persons earning less than $20,000 a year. If one does not own a car because one is too poor, is a senior citizen or a student, obviously one would not pay that 18 cents a gallon excise tax, but one would still receive the energy tax credit. If one owned a car and earned less than $20,000 a year, the energy tax credit provided the equivalent of 24,000 tax free miles per year.
Thus, the position of the government on this 18-cent excise tax is to save the consumer who owns and drives a car and earns more than $20,000 a year. That is their position, but in the process they are penalizing those people who earn less than $20,000 a year and those who do not own cars. For example, they are penalizing senior citizens who use heating oil and have to keep the temperature up because of their age and, perhaps most of all, the student who does not own a car but will be saddled with the debt the government is incurring on his behalf.
Mr. Beigie of the C.D. Howe Institute stated in Calgary on april 30 the following:
We are leaving a very unattractive legacy to the children. We are borrowing from the future as a nation rather than investing in it.
Therefore, at best the government is shielding a select and generally well-off portion of Canadian consumers of petroleum products. That is at best, but even they might not be getting the protection the government claims. The government indicated that crude oil increases will be less than what we proposed in our budget. To rationalize that, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources a couple of weeks ago sent out his officials with a totally fallacious, dishonest analysis of the energy-pricing agreement which the government had reached with the province of Alberta. Fortunately and not surprisingly, the press interpreted it for what it was-a sham, a shell game, a totally dishonest attempt to misrepresent what in fact had happened. They are trying to justify price increases considerably in excess of what had been decided by the previous Conservative government.
In his mini-budget, the Minister of Finance said that their blended pricing system, this magic made-in-Canada system, will result in $1 billion less expenditures through the import subsidy program.

On Tuesday night in Toronto the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources thought that $2 per year for the industry was fine. If we just combine those two, we are already at a $4 per barrel increase this year. That is contrary to every promise made by that group over there, including the Prime Minister, during the election campaign.
That does not take into account the statement by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources on April 16 in the House when he stated that they intended to collect from any oil-pricing agreement as much revenue as the previous government would have received from the budget of December 11. That means there will have to be an additional price increase this year of between $1 and $4 depending on whether or not the excise tax is included.
To honour the statements made by this government so far, it will require an increase in crude oil this year of between $5 and $9 a barrel, or twice as much as was provided for in the December 11 budget. That is a total contradiction of what this government pledged during the campaign. Remember, none of these figures takes into account any extra revenue for industry or any extra revenue for the government of Alberta. This does not take into account the position of the government of Alberta or the government of Saskatchewan, that they expect as much revenue out of the future pricing agreement as was provided for in the last budget.
What does that mean? Quite simply it means that if the Prime Minister, the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources were telling the truth to the House and to the country, then what can be expected out of an oil-pricing agreement for Canada is that the consumers of gasoline will be faced with price hikes at least as high-perhaps a penny or two less-as those which would have been provided by the December 11 budget. But what is truly shocking is that users of heating oil will be faced with much higher increases than provided under the December 11 budget, and there is no provision for tax credits for those who do not have a car.
The hon. member over there must have a giant V-8 that he is worried about filling up. How about worrying a little bit about the senior citizen who does not have a car but uses heating oil to heat his home? How about worrying a little bit about him?

speechtext:
The first thing to note, Mr. Speaker, is that this made-in-Canada price will mean that from its implementation, as soon as we have this made-in-Canada price, the price in Canada will increase immediately when OPEC prices increase. That is what will happen when this made-in-Canada price comes in. This so-called made-in-Canada price means the Government of Canada is going to get out of the responsibility for oil prices in this country. It is a cop-out. Why did the government adopt this scheme? I suggest it was for just that reason. I know the source of that scheme. I know where it came from. It was sold to this government. The government says: "Look, this is great, we put in this blended price system and if OPEC prices go up we just pass it along to the consumer and we do not take the blame. We can blame the Arabs."
This made-in-Canada price means the Government of Canada no longer takes responsibility for oil price increases in Canada. I know who passed this idea on to that great committee that made the decision over the Christmas holidays. Where did they get it from? This blended price, this made-in-Canada price, is precisely what was in effect in the United States in 1971. This blended price is what the Americans put in place in 1971.
What was the experience in the United States with this blended pricing system? It was a complete and utter disaster. After six or seven years of experience with this blended pricing system, the United States, about a year and a half ago, abandoned it because it found that it created chaos, confusion and required a bureaucracy of over 4,000 civil servants to administer. Let me read what the U.S. comptroller-general said, and I quote:
The cost is higher consumption, lower domestic production and higher imports. The program is complex, subject to fraud and manipulation and often administered ineptly.
That is what he said about this blended price, made-in-Canada, and stolen from the United States program.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, this government, this tired, old, dishonest bunch, would have the Canadian public believe that it will produce a made-in-Canada crude oil price by introducing a blended pricing scheme which the United States employed for six or seven years and has recently discarded because it was a disaster as an energy pricing policy. It makes one want to

May 8, 1980
Energy Policy
weep. Small wonder that the C.D. Elowe Institute in Montreal concludes that this government's energy-pricing policies are the greatest threat facing Canada today.
Aside from the dishonesty of this energy-pricing statement, the most damning criticism, and the real tragedy and the neglect and dishonesty of this minister, is that every single observer of the international energy situation has reached the conclusion that the real problem facing the world is not the price of oil, but will there be enough oil. Within two or three years the Soviet Union, the largest producer of crude oil in the world, will be a net importer of oil. This will mean that all of eastern Europe will be making demands on the same production the west is now making demands on, and there is not enough to satisfy our needs. No one but a raving maniac would suggest that international supplies of crude oil will remain readily available. In the face of that kind of world picture, it is clearly insanity for any nation to pursue policies that will increase our dependency on international supplies of oil. Yet that is precisely what the Government of Canada is doing.
By moving to this blended pricing scheme the government is adopting a scheme that leads to lower levels of domestic production and higher levels of imports. This is a scheme which exacerbates our already serious balance of payments problems, causing pressure on the dollar with resulting high interest rates and/or high inflation, which means that billions of Canadian dollars, instead of being ploughed back into the Canadian economy, will end up in the already overloaded coffers of middle eastern sheikhs. In the words of Marshall Crowe, a former adviser to the Liberal government and former chairman of the National Energy Board, we will end up with the worst of both worlds; high priced and scarce oil.
This government, instead of encouraging and promoting the development of new tar sands and heavy oil plants, has unilaterally acted to revoke a contract with Syncrude, producing at best only one year's delay at a cost of $2 billion to Canada, but perhaps causing the shelving of any other plans, certainly the delaying of any other plans for future Syncrude and heavy oil plants.
I am completely and continually amazed that this government has not worked out the simple fact that three tar sands of heavy oil plants would make this country self-sufficient. Furthermore, if we had them the money we would save would not be sent to the Middle East but would pay for those plants in three years. The NDP would rather send it to the Middle East because it might be some foreign owned company that would build them. They would sooner send it to the Middle East and let the sheikhs have it than build the plants in Alberta.
The real tragedy is the opportunity we are missing. Money spent here in Canada creates jobs here in Canada. We can continue the policy of this government relying on offshore supplies, relying on the Middle East, Mexico and Venezuela, or we can decide to become self-sufficient. That will cost a lot of money. It will mean tremendous changes in cash flows and distribution in this country, but that will have to be addressed. Again quoting Marshall Crowe:
The problem for Canada could be to decide what to do with its potential surplus rather than the problem of finding the foreign exchange to buy increasingly scarce oil from abroad.
In closing, I would like to make a plea to this government. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is behaving like the minister responsible for DREE. He says he wants to equalize things, forgetting entirely that he is the only minister in this government who has the responsibility for understanding that Canada has supplies of energy. What does it matter if we all share the shortages? What does it matter if we have some scheme in Canada for sharing the shortages when in fact we could and should have all the oil produced in this country to satisfy our needs, to be self-sufficient and to be unique in the world in that regard? My plea to the government is, stop this stupidity, stop fighting with the producing provinces, stop fighting with these bogeymen, the multinational oil companies, and get on with the job of making the country self-sufficient.
Then we can truly have a made-in-Canada oil price because we will not have to rely on the rest of the world. Then we can address the question and make sure that Canadians share equitably in the revenues generated by the tremendously healthy economy at that point of time. Let us do that, but for goodness sake let us get our priorities straight.
As every sensible and sane observer in the international community knows-I am not talking about partisan politicians or oil company executives but about the independent groups- our supply will not last. An MIT study of three years ago shows we face a crisis perhaps within the next two or three years, certainly no later than 1985. Yet the government is saying that the important question is 18 cents a gallon for car drivers earning more than $20,000 a year, that the important question is whether or not it can beat the producing provinces into submission or whether or not PetroCan will dig the holes or do something else. Those are not the important questions. The important question is: Will we have enough energy to heat our homes and drive our cars, no matter what the cost? That is the question and it is about time we had a minister of energy who will address himself to it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO FORMULATE HONEST AND EFFECTIVE ENERGY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the rhetoric of the two previous speakers has led me to think that we are back prior to February 18, engaged once again in hearing the same cant which we heard from the Conservative party and to some degree from the New Democratic Party during the campaign. What is equally evident, however, is that the House is conscious that Canada is part of a world faced with serious disequilibrium between supply and demand for oil.
Security of oil supply has become a major international problem. The fear about the security of supply, as much as lack of supply, leads to higher oil prices. There was no oil shortage in 1979, yet the fear of one led companies and governments to stockpile, driving prices up. Indeed, the price of oil rose in 1979 in relative terms on the same scale that it did during the Arab oil embargo of 1973-74. Massive price
May 8, 1980

increases in such an essential commodity as oil have, of course, substantial adverse economic effects. They increase the rate of inflation, decreasing the rate of world economic growth.
Canada is naturally not immune from that world reality. As a major trading country our own economic well-being depends on the economic health of the rest of the world. But Canada fortunately is in a unique situation. We are a net exporter of energy. We are a country rich in many natural resources and rich in people who know how to use those resources. Provincial public utilities have an outstanding track record in hydroelectricity and thermal generation of electricity, including nuclear. In the Canadian nuclear power system, for example, we have one of the most efficient and safest systems in the world. In non-conventional oil extraction, Canada has recently become a world leader.
However, these opportunities also confront us with many challenges. We are intent on making sure that our natural resources are used for the benefit of all Canadians and of the Canadian economy. We must be certain that we have increased energy supplies at prices people can afford. That is why we as a government will not tie ourselves to international prices, as the minister has repeatedly pointed out.
We are committed to the principle that all Canadians must benefit from our energy opportunities. Producing provinces have a clear entitlement to their natural resources. We undertake that they will get a fair return. But we are also committed to the principle that the federal government must have sufficient revenue to allow it to carry out its basic responsibilities of economic stabilization across our whole country. We are confident that all Canadians share the basic objective that energy will be used toward an equitable distribution of income.
We are confident, too, that the negotiations on oil pricing with Alberta will do nothing to affect adversely the principles of equalization and central management of our national economy. The petroleum industry in Canada has benefited enormously from higher oil prices. There is a broad consensus that the industry cash flow would have been enough had domestic oil prices risen only $2 a year. There is a real danger that too great a cash flow could result in bidding up the cost of production, increasing company takeovers and diversifying oil companies into other areas of economic activity.
Our policies will accordingly address the real possibility of excess concentration, as well as the degree of foreign control in our petroleum industry. The former Liberal government ensured that foreign ownership was reduced in that industry from 91 per cent to 75 per cent. This government will ensure that that total is further reduced to 50 per cent.
We in Canada are blessed with a variety of energy resources within our borders in addition to oil and natural gas. There is the tar sands, coal, uranium, hydroelectric capacity and so on. Accordingly, it would be shortsighted to allow our debate today to be dominated by the question of oil pricing.
While the energy problem may have arisen largely due to external factors, we believe that the remedies are within our own grasp. Regardless of what price is established for oil and
Energy Policy
gas on a domestic or international stage, we face now the fact of increased cost and difficulty in exploiting our non-renewable resources and, concurrently, the development of new sources of renewable energy.
It is that subject to which I should like to turn now. In order to facilitate the transition to alternative energy forms, this government is acting now to ensure a secure future for Canadians. At the same time, we have a responsibility to minimize social dislocation and adverse environmental impact.
I should like to say something about what we must do to increase the efficiency with which we use energy in order to reduce the rate of growth of our energy consumption. I want also to set forth some alternative sources of energy which we as a government are sponsoring.
First, what have we done and what may be done to foster conservation? Although there is likely to be an increased number of private vehicles on the roads of Canada in the near future, we can hold gasoline consumption stable by implementing fleet average performance standards for vehicles sold in Canada and encourage greater public use of mass transit, which would progressively lead to more efficient use of fuel. Another obvious conservation measure is insulation, whereby energy consumption in residences can be improved by an average of 37 per cent. CHIP, the Canadian Home Insulation Program established by the government in 1977, has already committed over $1 billion to this goal over the next seven years. Much, however, remains to be done to improve upon the insulation standards governing the construction of new residential units.
Our current practices in heating are wasteful in the extreme. With an oil-fired furnace, for example, we can reduce consumption by some 20 per cent through relatively simple means. Similar savings can be found in commercial and industrial buildings. Through design innovation and by replacing primary energy with waste energy, industry is becoming more secure and more competitive.
The government has shown leadership with a wide variety of programs directed toward this end. I am happy to report that we are working with private industry in demonstrating the various possibilities of conserving energy. The voluntary task forces of businessmen have already made major progress in this area. To demonstrate better the depth of our commitment, the federal government has embarked upon major internal programs for conservation which have already saved some $50 million annually.
Through other programs, our government funds district heating feasibility studies which estimate that a large central furnace burning conventional fuels can achieve an efficiency quotient of about 85 per cent, against much smaller ranges available for standard furnaces. The central heating sources would be particularly suitable for demonstrating the substitution of municipal and wood waste. In this case we would happily avoid the cost and environmental impact of garbage landfills.

May 8, 1980
Energy Policy
I have, through this brief selective survey, indicated our commitment to energy conservation. But second, and of equal importance, we shall take the opportunity to supply up to 10 per cent of our energy requirements from unconventional renewable energy. Most of this will come from the use of wood waste already accumulated in our forest industry. Wind and tidal energy are long-range potentials, but closer to realization are solar and biomass.
The federal government has a major role to play in developing solar, biomass, and nuclear energy. It undertakes longterm, high-risk developments which cannot be expected to be supported solely by the private sector. It also supplements work in this area by the provinces. As early as 1974, we established an interdepartmental task force, which evolved into an energy R and D panel, which apportions funds in relevant areas. Three-quarters of the total money sustaining the work in renewable energy, which was $21 million in the current fiscal year, comes through this panel. If we include expenditures of provincial governments and of private industries, the total swells to $35 million for renewable energy.
The National Research Council has taken a vigorous, effective lead in supporting, both within its own resources and in the private sector, new ventures in solar, tidal and wind energy. Much of this funding is contracted out to the private sector, with the National Research Council continuing to act as agent and scientific authority.
The heating of domestic water with solar energy is already cost-effective in Atlantic Canada. We have been active in promoting solar research and development through PASEM- a Program of Assistance to Solar Energy Manufacturers, and PUSH, the Purchase and Use of Solar Heating program. With the provinces, we have begun to demonstrate through these two programs the practicalities of solar energy.
With regard to biomass, Canada's vast forest and agricultural resources could, in theory, provide a huge amount of methanol annually. To equate this to current gasoline consumption, methanol could substitute for about 75 per cent of demand. Converting wood to gas is, however, still in its technological infancy, but we are working to establish its reliability and economy. Ethanol, from low grade wheat and other grains, is simple to produce but is currently economically unattractive. Our government has, therefore, created some $150 million in loan guarantees to assist in establishing electrical facilities using biomass as the energy source.
Finally, we have in Canada a nuclear industry with a product, the Candu reactor, of which we can all be proud. Here we have a high technology, indigenous Canadian industry which employs, directly and indirectly, some 85,000 Canadians. In a country which unfortunately lags behind its industrial competitors in much R and D, in a country where much of the industrial sector is passive branch plants, the Canadian nuclear industry is almost unique.
Nobel Laureat Albrecht Bethe said of the "technical wonder", the Candu reactor:
Not only is it very conservative in fuel usage, but it works with a regularity and reliability that are absolutely fantastic.
Compared with their major competitor coal, nuclear reactors are quiet, clean and reliable. They produce no smoke, no dust, no acid rain, no ash. Given the grave implications of the acid rain problem, we must use less harmful energy sources, and I include nuclear power as one.
Our energy strategy, then, is a multi-faceted one. We shall approach the time when there is a need to provide greater co-ordination of all these efforts which build bridges to a secure and prosperous future.
The problem, as I see it, in the area of renewable energy is twofold. First, how do we provide a public focus for these many activities currently under way? Second, how may we overcome the natural reluctance of lending institutions to finance new and risky technologies?
One approach, as the minister mentioned today, is the establishment of an alternative energy corporation, able to underwrite demonstration and commercial ventures of private companies by financial and technical assistance. It can undertake alternative energy projects, from the research stage through to commercial production. An alternative energy corporation will, in the public interest, share with private entrepreneurs the risks and benefits. It will, in addition, ensure that Canadians are protected from more mature foreign competitors. Initially, Petro-Canada, our own creation, will foster this fledgling corporation until it is old enough to go it alone.
I have covered a number of areas regarding conservation and renewable energy sources. Other speakers on this side of the House will deal with other questions, including the expansion of our national oil corporation, Petro-Canada.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to underline the exciting possibilities to which the minister drew attention-possibilities which can ensure all Canadians a stable and prosperous future.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO FORMULATE HONEST AND EFFECTIVE ENERGY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate on the motion presented by my colleagues condemning the government's failure to formulate an honest and effective energy policy. Let me say immediately that I support the motion and I agree wholeheartedly with both its letter and its spirit: the government has been both dishonest and ineffective in energy policy.
I intend to address my remarks today primarily to consumers across Canada and wish to consider how the government's failure affects these Canadians. Today, for Canadian consumers the price of energy is a vital issue. Consumers responsible for home heating costs and the cost of electricity face a perilous and potentially disastrous future in terms of matching their personal incomes to their expenditures for essential goods and services.
Their plight is compounded if they are also commuters required to travel by automobile to their employment. Those who live in the colder regions of Canada, the air conditioned city centres or those in areas where electrical generation is oil fueled, face special problems. They all stand on the brink of
May 8, 1980

financial disaster. Was the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) addressing Canadian energy consumers when he said: Welcome to the eighties?
Let us examine the great body of Canadians who are often referred to as "consumers". This group includes all 24 million Canadians in one sense, but there are some who buy more goods, supplies and services than others. In total number there are over 18 million in the adult Canadian group.
Let us take home owners, the group that would have been insulated against increasing costs for mortgage interest and municipal property taxes. Our mortgage interest and tax rebate program would have resulted in annual income tax savings of as much as $1,500 for these taxpayers. Now, those with mortgages face expense increases as high as $200 per month on loans in the $50,000 range without any help from the government.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) says there is no problem. Home owners, he says, can afford a drastic increase in interest rates. He says over 340,000 home owners who will be forced to pay increased interest rates will use only 30 per cent of their income for their monthly payment. That is no problem: they can cut back on luxury items like meat and potatoes. He says those 7,000 to 10,000 Canadians who are not disqualified by this cruel means test will be helped. He has not said how or when, so we must await the presentation of this limited assistance plan. In the meantime, some may lose their homes through foreclosures and the plan may never come about.
Mr. Speaker, there are 4.4 million occupant-owned homes in Canada. Many of those home owners face, or will face, increases in mortgage payments and property taxes in addition to substantial increases in normal household expenses. Of the seven-million-plus Canadian dwellings, 62 per cent are owned by the occupant. But those home owners-those elite Canadians, as the Prime Minister calls them-those rich people who can afford to bear cost increases according to the Deputy Prime Minister, are not the only ones who will suffer. Every Canadian family living in rented premises, and there are three million of them, faces the same kind of cost escalation, although not always directly in the form of interest rate and tax increases.
But hon. members can be certain that every interest payment, tax or utility charge increase will be recovered from the tenants. All seven million Canadian householders face the same interest, tax and household expense squeeze one way or another without help from the government. Their situation is now compounded because they have to face the energy problem. Seven million households are now being hit by the international energy crisis, and the government has no protection for them. The government has no policy to help them. That is why my colleagues condemn the government. The government has no policy on energy.
But the situation is worse than I have already indicated. Those seven million Canadian householders must participate
Energy Policy
in society and must work. By Canadian standards, they are entitled to recreation. But for many, the only method of transport is the private motor car. There again, Canadians face gloom and doom. The price of gas will rise. We ask, by how much? Not by as much as the PC government would have increased the price, says the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). How much is that? That depends, he is not sure, or so he says.
I am sure that, like death and taxes, gas price increases are inevitable. Gas prices will rise whether by way of an excise tax increase, a new wellhead price per barrel, a made-in-Canada price system, or any other formula. The most the government intends to do is to make the increase one or two pennies less than the gas price we announced last December. The government is only doing that so it will not be laughed at or scoffed out of office. The government does not intend to preserve the purity of the Liberal party promise not to increase the price of gasoline, only the technical words.
But what of the spirit of the promise? What of the Liberal party's vow to protect Canadians from the whims of the Ayotollah Khomeini? These people are lost in a sea of verbal rhetoric and mathematical mischief, deceit and dishonesty. Who are the victims? They are the ten million registered car owners in Canada, many of whom expected to pay much less for gas, not almost the same or even more, under a Liberal government.
We talk of consumer revolt. People are fed up with price increases. They naturally react favourably to promises to hold the line, to stabilize the price of gasoline, fuel oil and other forms of energy. The NDP spouted their usual rash promises of no price increases, lots of exploration and development without charge or sacrifice. But the NDP does not fool knowledgeable Canadians.
But Canadians were deceived by this government. There is no policy for price stability. There is no help. And, worst of all, there is no government respect for our seven million Canadian householders, our ten million car owners; that is to say, our Canadian consumers. If these people revolted, no army in creation could stop their advance. But fortunately for the government, Canadians are not like that. They are both peaceful and patient. They have been cruelly deceived. They face an uncertain increase in gas prices and fuel oil. They do not know the cost of energy, but they will wait until a policy or some kind of plan is formed.
What can Canadian consumers expect? Canadians must recognize the problems that face our nation in the energy field. We have a double-barrelled concern in Canada, namely supply and price. We can produce and purchase all kinds of energy at world prices, but that would adversely affect our whole economy. Yet if we continue to utilize our oil resources at current rates without provision for exploration and development of alternate energy resources, we will very soon run out of cheap Canadian energy. We will be left high and dry and dependent upon the whims of foreign nations and international oil dealers.

May 8, 1980
Energy Policy
There is only one answer, and everyone in this House knows it. As a national policy we must establish energy self-sufficiency in Canada. We must formulate a plan to achieve self-sufficiency. Naturally such a policy and plan has a price tag. We presented just such a plan. Many consumers thought that the price was too high. I, for one, accept that verdict. But what can we do?
First, let us consider the problem in relation to gasoline used for transportation. I consider that the government should be concerned about the plight of the commuter, the person who must travel by private car to his or her employment. It is also reasonable to make provision for necessary incidental travel for those in urban areas not served by public transportation, and for those in rural areas. Many consumers in this category would be expected to travel 12,000 to 15,000 miles a year. With a price of $1.20 per gallon and allowing 20 miles per gallon, the yearly gas supply would approximate $720. A 10-cent per gallon increase adds another $60 or more to the annual cost of transportation. Under the government's proposal, we can expect an annual increase of at least $200 for commuting consumers.
Can this increase be absorbed by them? I have serious doubts that the commuting consumer whose family income is in the $20,000 range has the income to cover this cost increase. Some provision must be made for financial assistance. We provided exactly that kind of assistance with our energy tax rebate.
A family of five would have received a rebate of approximately $250. Has the Minister of Finance made such a provision for rebate or for equivalent assistance? No, there is no help on the way. The government is content with keeping the increase one or two pennies below the price that we proposed. This is not much of a deal for consumers.
Let us look at the plight of those home owners or renters who are responsible for home heating costs. In Canada we have become used to a standard that has developed over the years which has allowed us to heat our homes to certain temperatures with a certain consumption of oil or gas, or whatever is used to heat the home. This past standard has to be reviewed in the light of current problems. Energy conserved is money saved.
Does the government become realistic with the people and tell them what the situation is? Does the government encourage people in this way or does it lead them on into thinking that they can go on and on using energy without a policy of conservation? It is true that an insulation program was instituted, but that was only a drop in a bucket compared to running a home at a temperature of 75 or 80 degrees fahrenheit. The government has to deal with these problems.
Cost has become a real concern to home owners. The cost of heating a home with approximately 1,200 square feet, say a bungalow in eastern Canada, is in the vicinity of $850 a year. Home owners can expect this cost to increase by approximately 20 per cent, which is nearly $200. How is the home owner going to absorb that cost without any assistance if his income is less than $20,000? I do not believe he can, and I believe that
the government must provide a program to assist that home owner.
We must remember that home heating costs affect groups of citizens. It is not, as the Prime Minister indicated in the past, that home owners are rich people. We have senior citizens, couples on old age assistance, who are trying to maintain themselves in their own homes. We have young families bearing all the cost of educating and clothing their children. They face these dramatic increases in cost too.
It is not realistic to think that these people can survive without some assistance from government. The Prime Minister and his ministers have said many times that they do not expect to ride on the backs of the poor, that they are not going to charge the increases in the cost of energy to the poor people in Canada. But they have provided no provision for subsidy. They have provided no program and no plan. 1 think it is improper. I think a plan has to be prepared.
Where will the money come from for a program of assistance to home owners in the lower income provinces? In Canada we spend over $2 billion a year subsidizing the importation of foreign oil. Much of this foreign oil is refined into gasoline for use in motor vehicles across Canada. Some of these cars with large engines use excessive amounts of gasoline, yet we subsidize them along with gas used in cars of lesser power with more economical engines. This is a terrible waste of funds. Then, too, we have all heard about border sales as a result of which subsidized gasoline is carried away across the border, again at tremendous cost to the Canadian taxpayers. There are many ways in which the system could be tightened so as to reduce the amount of money spent on subsidizing foreign oil imports. This money could be channeled into assistance required by home owners.
Let us talk for a moment about alternate supplies of energy because this is the long-term solution to the problem of the Canadian home owner-consumer in terms of the price of energy. Our program provided for funds to be rechanneled into vital energy projects thus reducing dependence, particularly in eastern Canada, upon imported oil.
Since the Liberal government was returned to office, all the programs that were vital to eastern Canada, particularly to Nova Scotia, have been stalled. The Donkin coal mine project which would have produced millions of tons of energy to replace foreign oil is adrift. Nothing is being done. The government has done nothing to speed up the extension of the natural gas pipeline eastward. The matter is presently before the National Energy Board and some interest has been expressed in its extension, but there are many things the government could do to advance this vital and important project. While there is afoot a project involving the Annapolis River, much research remains to be done in the development of tidal power in the Bay of Fundy. All these projects, including things like solar energy mentioned by the parliamentary secretary, are vitally important to the long-range effect on consumers because they are the method by which we can reduce
May 8, 1980

dependency on foreign oil and thus reduce the cost of energy to consumers, particularly in eastern Canada.

Mr. Speaker, if the people of Halifax with a 1977 or 1978 Chevrolet fill up today it costs them slightly more than $20 whereas if they had to pay the international price the people in Halifax West would have to pay twice as much. It is the security of supplies which is somewhat uncertain and which wavered at the end of 1978 and the beginning of 1979. European or Asian visitors to Canada would think that there is absolutely no oil shortage in Canada,
even if we consider oil prices and supplies, while everywhere else such a shortage exists and causes problems for the industry.
This Canadian policy has also contributed to ensuring the survival of our industries in the east, both in Quebec and in the Atlantic provinces, which means that they are in a much better position than their competitors in Europe, Asia or Japan, because they are guaranteed supplies at a much lower price than the world prices.

Some provincial governments may not have recognized the need to share their wealth with the rest of Canadians, but this need is becoming more and more obvious. Under our constitution the Government of Canada has the right, and 1 submit the duty, to ensure that goods, including obviously hydro power, pass freely from one province across the territory of any other-

Mr. Speaker, in my introductory remarks before the dinner hour I said that the energy question touched upon many different challenges facing the country in the 1980s such as the constitutional problems and the foreign ownership problems. Our view in December was that the proposals put forward by the Conservative government of the day did not lead to a resolution of those problems, but compounded them. So, we believe that we must, as Canadians, attempt to find a solution. I impress upon the House the fact that we in this party are under no illusions as to how difficult that search will be. We must find a solution that will strengthen our economic independence and not weaken it, that will strengthen Canada's long-range industrial and economic future rather than weaken it.
I am sure most Canadians are aware that Canada imports oil. Somewhere in the area of 20 per cent of its oil needs are met by foreign suppliers, for which we pay a world price at the moment in excess of $30, and we charge Canadians about half that amount. The majority of the oil produced in Canada in 1980 is what is known as conventional oil, but the fact remains that our conventional supplies are rapidly depleting and will have to be replaced by far more expensive non-conventional supplies of which the tar sands are perhaps the most well-known example.
In determining a policy on energy pricing, we must consider the fact that there is a distinction between old oil and new oil, and that nearly all of the existing conventional petroleum reserves-more than 96 per cent of them-were discovered prior to 1973. The fact remains that the majority of the oil we are using today is the same as the oil on which companies in 1972 or 1973 were making a 15 per cent rate of return. At that time the price per barrel was $2.77. Even allowing for the fact that operating costs may have risen more than $1 per barrel on conventional oil, which still provides the majority of the supplies we use in Canada, if we do not change our taxation and royalty systems in relation to any increases in price which take place from this day on, the fact remains that we will be draining off to the multinational companies some $2 per barrel, or $1.3 billion per year. We must ask ourselves whether that is the kind of policy we want to follow. We rejected the view in December, and we reject it today.
The problem remains that the Liberals are telling us they believe in something called the blended price. Apparently a combination of the price of conventional oil, the price of
imported oil and the price of non-conventional supplies are somehow put into a blender to produce a mixed price. I see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans) laughing. I am sure, since he is a former professor of economics, he will be able to explain to this House, the way he was able to explain to his students, exactly what a blended price consists of. I would suggest to you that it is simply a way of attempting to justify to the Canadian people an increase whose size may not be justified by the requirements of the cost of production.
There are arguments which we on this side are prepared to accept for some increase in the price of oil as we enter the 1980s.

speechtext:
I have not come to criticize you. You are very sensitive. It is not a question of criticism, it is a question of analysing the basis on which the Liberal party is going to be giving us these tremendous price increases, and analysing where these revenues are going to go and how they are going to be recycled.
The fact of the matter is that, even on the Liberals' own terms, if we follow the policy of the Liberal party of eventually gaining 50 per cent control of our oil and natural gas, which is the objective the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has set for the country, the dividends which will be leaving the country as a result of price increases and as a result of windfall profits to multinational companies, that have by far the greatest stake, not only in our non-conventional supplies but in our conventional supplies, will amount to tens of billions of dollars.
