May 8, 1980

The fact of the matter is that it is not possible to go to the Canadian people and ask them to accept higher prices for oil and natural gas when they know what the cost of conventional supplies is, and when they know where the windfall profits are going. That is the critical problem. The problem is not so much a question of price; the problem is a question of revenue and where the revenue goes.
As I said earlier, whereas the Liberal party has been using this particular problem as an excuse, in a sense, for mobilizing certain sentiments in central Canada against those of the west, we take the view in our party that we have to find a way, in terms of our constitution, to provide for a solution to the energy crisis which will, at one and the same time, recognize the legitimate rights of producing provinces, and they have rights to some revenues from increases in prices, and indeed from existing prices, and provide for the generation of surplus within Canada which will provide for future energy needs.
We took the position in December that the excise tax was wrong in December, and we take the position that the excise tax is wrong today. The excise tax is not the way in which to go about punishing the consumer in order to generate revenues for the federal government. If anything has emerged in the past four weeks since this Elouse began sitting, it is that the government itself has no particularly clear idea of how it is going to replace the Tory excise tax. Indeed, there was an interesting ambiguity in the throne speech. That ambiguity was in saying not that there will be no excise tax, which was the promise the Prime Minister made to the Canadian people when he was campaigning for office, but that there will be no 18-cent excise tax, which is the new position of the Liberal party.
There is a very major difference between going to the Canadian people and saying there will be no excise tax, and coming back to the Canadian people and saying in the throne speech there will be no 18-cent excise tax. What are we waiting for from the Liberal government, a 17-cent solution, or a 16-cent solution?
We have been convinced for some time that we have to deal with the problem of windfall profits, profits that are substantial both in the United States and in Canada. The fact of the matter is that oil profits in the first quarter of this year have been higher than ever before in Canada's history, and that they are on average 100 per cent higher than they were for the first three months of 1979.
If the Canadian people are going to be paying more for their oil and for their natural gas, they want the assurance that those prices and those revenues are not simply being recycled and taken out of the country. The evidence today is that this is precisely what is happening as a result of pricing policies, as a result of free enterprise policies, and as a result of multinational oil company policies, policies which were followed by the Conservative government when it was in power, and policies which are being followed by the Liberal government today. That is why the question of public ownership is not some ideological ruse simply coming from those who seek public ownership for its own sake.
Energy Policy
Public ownership in this particular field is a necessity because it is the one key which will give to the Canadian people the knowledge and the confidence that when they are paying more for their gas at the pump, that money is being recycled into the Canadian economy and being used by Canadians for Canadians. It is simply not possible to divide up revenues in such a way that will satisfy the producing provinces, the multinational oil companies, the needs of the federal government and the needs of all the people of Canada, without raising that price to a level which is completely unjustifiable. That is why the Conservative government fell in 1979, and that is the conundrum facing the Liberal party in 1980.
We have to recognize that the solution to this problem is not an easy one. Certainly we on this side recognize that. We wish the minister well in his negotiations with the provincial governments. We are not at all impressed with the information he has given us, or with the conflicting news inflicted on this Parliament week by week as we are told the government is not considering a certain tax. Then ministers come back the next day and say, "we are not considering that tax this year", or they criticize the Conservative party for its $4 or $4.50 increase, and yet indicate that the over-all package which the Liberal party may be proposing over the next three years may result in prices which are even higher. It is not a particularly impressive record. Certainly it is not a record of honesty and integrity in energy policy, which is what this motion is all about.
If new patterns of public ownership could be established in the oil industry, Canadians would see that revenues from higher prices were being used for exploration and development, conservation, and for the growth of alternative supplies. There would be no need to challenge provincial ownership of this resource. Furthermore, tremendous disparities in provincial revenues as a result of ownership of resources could be at least partially resolved by direct interprovincial transfers or by the funding of a national energy bank which could be drawn on as a source of capital by non-producing provinces.
I suggest that energy self-sufficiency would then be a goal which would provide some sinew to the new confederation, a confederation which would recognize the legitimacy of provincial economies without making of them a fetish, a confederation which would recognize the notion of sharing, the importance of national co-operation, strategic planning, intervention and, indeed, selective public ownership. Dare I call it a cooperative commonwealth?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this opposition day debate on energy. With the exception of the referendum in Quebec, I cannot think of an issue that is as important to the future of Canada as that of energy. When one comes to understand what the effect of the government's inaction in the field of energy may bring, it does not take too much foresight to imagine how difficult life may soon be.
862

May 8, 1980
Energy Policy
Television has already demonstrated what life with gasoline shortages will be like by showing us the American experience. Gas stations will close on Sundays, or at the end of the month when their supplies run low. People wishing to purchase gas will have to stand in line. Unrest will grow as farmers and truckers find that they no longer have the fuel that they need in order to earn their livelihood. Consumer goods based on hydrocarbons will inflate rapidly in value as supplies of oil for industry dwindle. Finally, the government will turn to rationing in order to ensure a fair division of remaining supplies.
Eventually, public opinion will force the government to examine alternative sources of energy and new methods of introducing conservation. That was the American experience. For Canada the scenario is just one step more severe. Unlike the United States, Canada does not have areas of warm climate. When our oil runs out, people will have to deal with the Canadian winter.
Let us assume that somehow the government comes to understand the problem and manages to provide an adequate supply of oil to heat our homes, drive our cars and fuel our industries. But no matter what expense we go to in order to search for new supplies of oil and gas, eventually we will run out. No need to worry; by then we will have switched to hydrogen-powered cars and our homes will be heated by electricity, solar power or biomass.
There are only a few small details to be ironed out. The new technologies that we will need to produce these forms of energy take time and considerable sums of money to create. Canada has proved to be unwilling to invest those sums. But this is just the beginning of the technology that we will need.
It is fine to discuss replacing the energy that we get from oil, but how do we begin to replace hydrocarbons in their other functions? For example, how do we replace oil as a lubricant or as a base in paint, or for its use in producing drugs? Or how do we replace the use of oil for producing plastics and other synthetics? We have an understanding of the means of producing new forms of energy so that the average Canadian will be able to drive his car and heat his home. However, the question remains, without oil will we be able to build that car or furnish that house?
If we were to look around and try to come to an understanding of how important oil is to the maintenance of our style of life, I think that we would come to realize just how undervalued our remaining supplies are. Granted, Canada does have larger oil reserves than Saudi Arabia. The question is, will we be able to get it out of the ground when we need it? Unless the government is willing to invest in heavy oil, the tar sands, frontier exploration and new delivery systems, the answer is no. Running out of oil seems like a remote possibility until one remembers that Alberta's conventional reserves will run out in less than ten years.
Getting oil from the tar sands is a costly venture and this government, under the guise of a made-in-Canada price, has said that it is unwilling to pay that price. The Liberal party referred to the last campaign as the "18-cent election". I wonder what the people of Canada will say when they recognize the real cost of their decision. The government has committed itself to rationing in the event there is shortfall in supply. It takes great pride in telling Canadians that this is the only fair way in dealing with distribution. Through rationing, it is explained, people would receive energy on the basis of need, not according to their ability to pay, and on those terms it does seem quite attractive.
What the government overlooks is that rationing will lead to as many problems as it solves. A black market in gasoline is sure to develop which will lead to a situation where those who have money will still be able to afford to drive, while those who could not afford the cost prior to rationing will be even less likely to be able to survive in the marketplace.
Which groups will be hardest hit by such a situation? It will be the poor, commuters, those who use fuel in the course of earning their living, people in rural areas who generally do not have access to mass transit and, of course, the elderly who will have low priority when it comes to allocating the rations, and who do not have the economic power to deal in the market.
There has been much made, Mr. Speaker, of federal-provincial antagonisms over resource control. There have been serious actions and reactions between Ottawa and the provinces, differences that at times seem to threaten our nation. At the very least natural resources are a focal point of constitutional discussions. It is important that this matter is approached openly and, indeed, it has been given scrutiny by a number of examiners. But there is a major feature of this rationing possibility that should give major concern to those interested in regional energy supplies and resource control. This rationing system would ultimately be an arm of the federal government.
How would the needs of industry be considered as compared to commuters and other private consumers? How would one province's needs be considered as compared to another? How much power would reside within the rationing bureaucracy in a country that remains 20 per cent dependent on foreign supplies of petroleum because it has failed to provide the dollars necessary for resource development and, in fact, continues to increase our national deficit by not even recovering the $4 billion of subsidy payments to offset the cost of foreign inputs?
Who will say, Mr. Speaker, whether I will do without gas because my function is not as important as yours and that you will do without gas because your function is not as important as a farmer's? Will we or will we not have gas? Should Parliament be dissolved so the farmer may plant? For all the energy problems we have addressed in the last years, our actions have been mere tokens of the real actions that are needed.

speechtext: How did they win the war?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO FORMULATE HONEST AND EFFECTIVE ENERGY POLICY
speechtext:
We did not have the New Democratic Party when the war was on. On past experience, I know that the bureaucracy has seldom shown the sort of insight that areas such as mine require.
I would like to turn now to an examination of the policy priorities of the Liberal and Conservative parties. 1 think a moment would be well spent in contrasting the records of the two parties while in power. This government is incapable of separating its often misguided notions of social justice from its other policy discussions. Its set of values tends to cloud its judgment. For example, in the May, 1976, budget the government introduced measures which would have imposed a special graduated excise tax on heavy cars. I am sure that the reason for introducing the measure was that the government had romantic notions about putting an end to limousines, at least for cabinet ministers-or at least other than for cabinet ministers. What the government failed to consider was the fact that such an excise tax would actually discriminate against many efficient cars. Under the scheme, a Camaro giving 18 miles per gallon would only be taxed $70, while a Cutlass of that model year using one gallon every 24 miles would be subject to a $500 tax levy. Fortunately public and opposition reaction caused the government to withdraw.
Let us consider the history of the government's conservation policies and targets. Between 1975 and 1979 the government announced three different target rates for growth of energy demand, and made energy conservation announcements a total of ten different times. This might seem to indicate that the government was being quite progressive and was introducing stronger and stronger measures. What it really means is that the government kept making announcements to contradict or change its previous announcements. For example, the government announced its program to label household appliances four different times during that period. I am optimistic enough to believe that we may some day see the results of those announcements.
Last fall the House heard lengthy speeches from the Liberal benches about the length of time that it was taking for a Conservative government to reach an agreement with the provinces regarding oil pricing and federal taxation. It is
Energy Policy
worthy of note that those remarks came from the same people who were stalled for three years, between 1973 and 1976, in similar negotiations, and from the same people who are practising confrontation with the west today.
Our government had reached an agreement with the west. It was an agreement which would have provided funds for a federal energy development bank. It was an agreement that would have promoted conservation of our non-renewable resources. It was an agreement that would have provided an impetus to the development of the tar sands and heavy oils. It was an agreement that would have set the stage for the development of alternate forms of energy. In short, it was an agreement that would have provided energy self-sufficiency and a future for Canada, and it was an agreement that this government has rejected.
Under Liberal governments, Canada has had to import ever-increasing shares of its oil requirements. The Canadian public has seen little or no action on extending the natural gas pipeline to Quebec and the maritimes. Renewable forms of energy have been largely ignored. The Canada reactor has languished because of poor marketing, scandals, and inconsistent standards for nuclear safeguards. In sum, the government has a miserable record. Its last target for energy conservation was to limit the growth in demand for energy to 3.5 per cent per annum. This sort of conservation leads to a doubling of Canada's energy requirements every 21 years.
Even when the government sees fit to introduce worth-while programs such as PASEM and PUSH, mentioned by the parliamentary secretary, it does not follow through to their full realization. The government creates programs, creates an industry, and then loses interest and allows the project to wither and die.
Even having seen what Liberal governments have done in the past I do not despair of Canada's ever seeing a coherent energy strategy. Quite the opposite, in fact. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) recently proved, the government knows where to go when it needs well reasoned and innovative policies. Because Canada benefits as a result of such a process 1 do not begrudge the government the use of our policies and, in fact, I would like to take this opportunity to remind them of some points that they may have overlooked in our platform.
The Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, as represented by its members in the House of Commons and its supporters across our country, has made no secret of its desire and willingness to see Canada become energy self-sufficient by 1990. In order to meet that target Canadians may have to face some short-term inconvenience, but what we receive in return is long-term security of supply. The pricing formula and budgetary means for such a program are well known and I will not dwell upon them. On the other hand, 1 would like to enumerate the areas of development that are essential to the completion of such a plan.
I was honoured to have been able to sit as a member of the prime minister's advisory committee on energy last summer. That committee was struck because our government inherited a legacy of inaction on energy matters. We needed to deter-

May 8, 1980
Energy Policy
mine what could be done to turn the situation around. The committee met throughout the summer and examined energy matters from the perspective of the provinces, of the various companies involved in energy development in Canada, and on the basis of the needs of the average Canadian. Reconciling those varied positions is difficult but it can be done, and we had made a start at doing so. An energy agreement has been worked out with the west, oil companies had been consulted about the price increases that they needed in order to bring new resources on stream, and the end result would have been an assured supply for all Canadians.
These measures grew out of the policies that we had outlined prior to the May 22 election. One cannot compare an election platform of one party that has not been in government for a considerable period of time with the legislative record of one that has. What one can compare, on the other hand, is the fact that the present government, in its previous incarnations, failed to come to terms with Canada's energy needs, while in the six months of our government a comprehensive energy program was outlined and we had taken steps to implement that program.
How did the last Liberal government come to terms with the need for conservation? It spent considerable sums of the taxpayers' money telling taxpayers how to conserve. It spent further sums training people as experts in energy conservation in order to run their taxpayer education scheme, and then cancelled the whole program. It then went on to set conservation targets for itself. In fact the department that was responsible for the program could not meet the target and, in fact, 17 departments actually increased their energy consumption in the same period. All of this was at even further expense to the taxpayer. Even though the government failed to save energy, it proved that in Canada there was a long way to go in conservation of tax dollars.
The bulk of the government's push for conservation is to be found in the CHIP program. CHIP has a number of problems of its own but it, at least, does provide some assistance to home owners. Unfortunately it has also caused a number of fly-bynight insulation companies to come into being.
By and large, the government has felt that conservation can be mainly voluntary. It is my opinion that voluntary conservation is about as likely as the individual Canadian deciding to do his part in fighting inflation by refusing his next pay raise. The fact of the matter is that he will only start to conserve when the price of energy starts to become a concern. Obviously the poor should not be pressed further into poverty by the cost of energy, nor should those living on fixed incomes be asked to bear a heavy burden. It is for that reason that our government introduced the energy tax credit in the Crosbie budget. The tax credit would have been more than equal to the increased cost of energy to those on low incomes. At the same time we were prepared to increase funding for CHIP, and I am pleased to see that the government has followed our example.
While conservation provides an immediate and vital decrease in our energy requirements, it does not fill all of our needs. We must, therefore, look to expanding our supply of
energy. Remembering that hydrocarbons may be too valuable merely to burn, we must look to alternate forms of energy to fill the gap, and to replace this finite resource.
Canada has leading edge technology in the field of nuclear energy. The Candu is at one and the same time the most productive reactor over its life cycle and the safest reactor in use in the world. This is a technology which could and should be exported in order to offset our balance of trade deficit. Unfortunately the government, through AECL, has not been able to market the system properly, and in the case of its deal with Argentina actually managed to lose money by selling a reactor.
In dealing with renewable energy, the government has had an equally poor record. It did institute the PASEM and PUSH programs, but it dumped those funds into the market so quickly that the industry could not take proper advantage of them. Now, after having tried to develop the industry, the government, in the Speech from the Throne, announces its intention to create a renewable energy corporation which would compete with the small companies and possibly lead to their demise. The government recently announced the composition and funding of this corporation. This is a gleam of hope after years of limited action.
By comparison, the Crosbie budget provided for lower bond requirements for individuals wishing to distill alcohol for fuel, provided for accelerated write-offs for conservation equipment, and established discounts on natural gas in order to persuade Canadians to convert from oil to gas furnaces. In effect, six months of Conservative government showed more of a conviction to deal with energy problems than the previous decade of Liberal government. The government shows little indication that it intends to mend its ways. It will continue to pretend that there is no problem until the lights go out.
Mr. Speaker, the concept of an energy crisis has gradually entered our consciousness. Indeed, we do have a problem, but it does not come from a lack of reserves; rather, the crisis is with the cost and the will necessary to identify, develop and distribute our God-given resources. The crisis cannot be met with the traditional manipulations, reactions and confrontations at different government levels. We have an immediate need to respond to the condition by developing a national policy, based on the regional opportunities that present themselves.
We must extend the neglected natural gas pipelines to provide markets and linkages for gas reserves, east to west, north to south. We must seriously consider the neglected electrical interconnection and controls to allow the vast quantities of electrical reserves in James Bay and Churchill Falls to be accepted in New York or Ontario grids. We must finally come to grips with the whole question of resource export taxation on natural gas, oil, as well as electrical energy.
Especially in those provinces whose opportunities to develop fossil reserves are limited, we must hesitate no longer to take major steps to provide opportunities for replacement of con-
May 8, 1980

ventional fuels. The government should take into account the British Columbia opportunity for a major coal liquefaction plant. Similar opportunities offer themselves in the Atlantic provinces.
Transportation fuels account for about 45 per cent of petroleum consumption. The potential of conversions from conventional fuels to natural gas and its components, including M gas and gasahol, have yet to be recognized by this government by appropriate taxing and bonding measures. In the prairies, Ontario, and Prince Edward Island, opportunities for synthetic fuel production from biomass or waste may have been delayed by this government's inaction.
Conservation can be enhanced not only by pushing through research and development of appropriate fuels and engines for private transportation, but also by major research and development and dedication to an improved urban transit system.
Our previous government had initiated a concept of funding for energy projects. That funding would have derived from revenue from energy resources. Without specific and major financial resources, major projects in cogeneration, urban transit, and tidal power may fail to materialize. Major conventional energy systems such as heavy oil supply, hydro development, and additional coal mining opportunities, may be delayed.
Because of the lack of a cohesive energy plan we continue to miss the opportunities for development of potential exportable energy technologies, such as those coming from research and development in photovoltaics and genetic engineering.
Financial research and development capability and political will should provide us a secure energy future. We are destined with the government's present approach to an increasing dependency on petroleum imports and increasing political antagonisms-a fossil-foolish mentality-that need not have limited our energy future.

speakeroldname: Mr. Russell MacLelian (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State, Mines):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Mines)
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO FORMULATE HONEST AND EFFECTIVE ENERGY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion there is no other point in the Speech from the Throne that was more welcome or more important than the one that dealt with the setting up of the alternate energy corporation. This is something which we in the Liberal party feel is going to be extremely valuable in the years to come, and one which we feel the party and the government will put to good use. It is hoped by each and every one of us, certainly by parliamentarians in general, that the alternate energy corporation will not only seek to find ways of using possible new sources of energy, but also will not discount or ignore the existing sources of energy that are in our country in such abundance.
It is one of those sources of energy that I would like to deal with this evening, namely, coal. This afternoon the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) discussed the problem that Nova Scotia has regarding is dependency on offshore oil. This dependency no doubt exists. In fact it has existed for some time. When we were blessed with an inexpensive source of oil, this was not a problem. But when the cost of offshore oil
Energy Policy
rose, and rose very quickly, it caught the province of Nova Scotia very much by surprise.
As the hon. member for Halifax West stated, dependency on offshore oil amounted to approximately 70 per cent of electrical generating requirements. Since that time there has been movement to reduce this particular dependency. The province of Nova Scotia has brought on stream a hydroelectric system in Wreck Cove, Cape Breton Island, and also four thermal generating plants at Lingan close to New Waterford. It is hoped when thermal generating plants three and four are on stream that this will reduce Nova Scotia's dependency on offshore oil from 70 per cent to approximately 15 per cent.
The uses and possibilities for coal are limitless. The use of coal is very important when we look at the possibility of finding alternate sources of oil and transportation fuels. The idea of liquefaction of coal, liquefying coal, or gasifying coal started in pre-war Germany, and the hydrogenation of coal is something that goes back quite a few years. Unfortunately it is something that has been neglected over the past because of the abundance of cheap energy, but it is now being looked at very seriously. Unfortunately it will take a good many years before the technology that was started so many years ago is brought on stream and made viable in Canada. We are anticipating that it will probably be the mid-1990s before this very valuable source of oil is available to us.
There is another source that was started at approximately the same time, that is, the sasol process which was developed in pre-war Germany as well, but has been adopted in South Africa. It is a process that the South Africans initiated in 1953 with the building of Sasol One. It is a process for the liquefaction of coal using an adjustment of the carbon monoxide hydrogen components and, using a catalyst, in fact can form a very wide abundance of products ranging all the way from methane to a heavy petroleum wax. It is a very strong and excellent possibility for the future, not only for South Africa but for the world as a whole.
Just a few days ago Sasol Two was commissioned in South Africa and a trade delegation from Canada was there at this particular exercise. This new plant is capable of producing
45,000	barrels of oil a day from the coal derivative. South Africans are going to be commissioning a third sasol plant, and that will be commissioned in 1983.
In 1983, when Sasol One, Two and Three are working, they will in fact be producing 50 per cent of all of South Africa's transportation fuels. This is a significant portion of the country's transportation fuel needs, but of course it will utilize a great deal of coal. The fact is that these two plants, one producing 45,000 barrels of oil a day from coal, and the second producing 50,000 barrels a day from coal, will require as much as 27 million tonnes of coal a year. This is more coal than is produced in Canada at the present time. Yet it is a need in this country. It exemplifies to us what a valuable resource this is and how we are going to come to depend on this very valuable resource.
The South Africans are able to utilize this source of energy right now because of cheap labour costs. They are able to

May 8, 1980
Energy Policy
produce coal for about $6 a ton, which is considerably cheaper than Canada can. The plant that will be coming on stream in 1983 they expect will cost between $3 billion and $4 billion. The Fluor Corporation which has constructed Sasol Two, and will be constructing the third one, is in fact negotiating with the American government at the present time to construct the plant in that country. The Americans are showing considerable interest in this technology. That corporation estimates that the plant, capable of producing 50,000 barrels of oil a day from coal, will in fact cost $3.5 billion. In terms of comparing this to a refinery producing oil from oil sources, it would be the equivalent of $48 a gallon-

speechtext:
-a barrel. Although we have not reached the situation where coal is in a position to compete with oil in the gasoline markets, we are going to be fast approaching that point. It is something we are very definitely going to have to consider.
Mobil Oil, also in the United States, has developed a process called Mobile M where they are able to turn coal into methanol and upgrade the methanol into a high octane gasoline by a process known as methanol M, and the product derived therefrom is known as M gasoline. In 1979 New Zealand found that using a natural gas base to create methanol would in fact give them a high octane gasoline at $10 a barrel cheaper than the gasoline which could be produced from the sasol derivative. They are using this process now and are producing gas from this source.
In the United States, because of their interest not only in the sasol process but in the Mobile M process, they have designated $100 million for exploration experimentation, and research into this valuable source of fuel for the future. They are making grants of $4 million each to companies, research laboratories and institutions of sufficient size to be able to carry out this valuable work. Applications for these grants closed on April 25 and the results should be announced in the not too distant future.
With respect to our country, the Alberta Gas Trunk Line has in fact sent two tons of coal to the Saarberg Corporation in Germany which has been very active in the hydrogenation of coal. This coal was experimented on there and fuel was produced from it. The cost to the Alberta Gas Trunk Line was merely the cost of the shipment because the Saarberg Corporation was able to do the work at very little cost to this country. The Alberta Gas Trunk Line is now in the process of carrying out detailed feasibility and conceptual engineering studies of this interesting possibility.
The Brazilians are using methanol in their automobiles. In fact all major automobile manufacturers in Brazil are making cars which run on methanol. These methanol-powered engines are becoming very popular, and it is estimated that in Brazil at the present time they have approximately 100,000 such cars. Methanol gives off a much cleaner exhaust and is a more
energy efficient fuel than high octane gasoline. The methanol rating would be approximately 103, whereas high octane gasoline would probably have a rating of about 93. In Germany, Volkswagen has developed a car which runs exclusively on methanol. There are other cars, including Volkswagens, which run on a combination of methanol and gasoline. So the technology is there; it is growing and becoming increasingly popular.
With respect to eastern Canada some difficulty arises because the coal is a little more expensive to extract from the ground, yet there is another technology which I think is going to be extremely important to eastern Nova Scotia, a process which the British are developing. As you probably know, Mr. Speaker, the coal in eastern Canada is very high in volatiles; approximately 20 per cent to 30 per cent of the coal in Cape Breton consists of volatiles.
The British are developing a process whereby the volatiles in such coal are separated by using a solvent. The carbon portion of the coal could be used for thermal generating and the volatiles for transportation fuel. Canmet is very involved in this particular situation, working on what is more or less the next step, and is developing what they call a hydrocracker, a process for upgrading heavy oils which would be the derivative of the solvent-producing carbon on the one hand and the heavy oil on the other. The heavy oil volatiles could then be used to be upgraded into a light oil capable of feeding any refinery which exists in this country at the present time. Not only that, but to this heavy oil could be added additional hydrogen and coal, coal solids, and this mixture could be upgraded to an efficient fuel capable of being fed into any refinery in the country. This is not new technology, it is technology which has existed for the past 17 years, but it is very important technology as far as eastern Canada is concerned. Unfortunately it has been allowed to languish unused for far too long a period.
It is hoped that the alternate energy corporation will bring this technology forward to a greater degree for the benefit not only of eastern Canada but of the whole of Canada, and that coal will become a very serious alternative in a fuel-hungry world. It is important to this country that we explore all our energy possibilities. The government has declared its intention to go ahead with the natural gas pipeline to Nova Scotia. They have made that commitment in the Speech from the Throne. It is a very important commitment when one considers the possibilities of natural gas existing off Sable Island.
Added to this is another possibility, the possibility of oil off the coast of Newfoundland. These are very important potential sources brought to prominence to a large extent through the contribution of Petro-Canada, an institution to which this government has pledged its support-in fact the government has made available to the corporation an extra $80 million, recognizing that this is an important operation upon which the satisfaction of the future energy requirements of this country is going to depend. It is important that sources of energy and sources of wealth are derived from all areas of this country and that no area should find its natural resources or its possibilities for employment pushed into the background.
May 8, 1980

All members here will agree that although we represent various constituencies we are also representatives of the whole country, and in this very important matter we must look not only to decisions which have been taken, but also those yet to come. On May 20 there will be made one of the most important decisions in the history of this country. But sometimes, before decisions can be made, problems must be overcome. We owe it not only to our constituents but to a unified country that these problems, and the areas in which these problems are found, are studied, analysed and understood. It is only in this way we, as a country, will become more unified and more purposeful.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO FORMULATE HONEST AND EFFECTIVE ENERGY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may 1 begin by saying that as a new member I am rather astounded at the situation in which we find ourselves today in Canada with regard to energy. It is inconceivable that we would be running out of a resource of which we have more in Canada than has ever been found in the world to date because past governments have not had the wisdom or the courage to develop these resources. The main reason I entered politics was to help bring some businesslike sanity into government and the
Energy Policy
ownership and better development of resources and responsible economic policies on which to build a great future for this country. Economic policy must involve energy these days, and energy policy must involve economics. They are interlocked and indivisible. One holds the key to the other.
We have known for a long time that we in Canada were energy rich and resource rich. We have known that by selling our resources we could live like kings without working very hard. Over three decades Liberal governments have capitalized on this fact to provide better social standards for Canadians, and that has been great up to a point, but such wealth must be carefully handled. It must be wisely utilized to provide not only social justice but also creative work for Canadians, and an investment in future stability, because resources do run out, many of them, and so some portion of their value must be set aside to build an ongoing industrial base for the benefit of future generations of Canadians who will follow us. However, successive governments have consistently spent more than they took in, and Canada has amassed a huge national debt, partly by buying foreign goods and services instead of letting Canadians produce them.
We have sold our raw materials, our iron ore, nickel, asbestos, tin, zinc, tungsten, oil and gas in great quantities and at low prices, and we have bought cars, televisions, cameras, machines and thousands of other manufactured goods at high prices. We have exported Canadian jobs and guaranteed the employment of foreigners. It is time we stopped doing this kind of stupid thing, stole a leaf from the Parti Quebecois book and became maitres chez nous\ masters of our own house, controllers and investors in our own destiny.
I would like to use my time to look at the benefits of energy development rather than dwell on just the costs, as the Liberal side of this House has myopically continued to do.
It is incumbent on any government of any country to plan for future needs, but for the government of a country as vast as Canada-and as subject to cold weather conditions as Canada is-not to have planned much, much better for energy development, is no less than dereliction of duty. However, that is the position we are in. No longer are we exporters of petroleum energy. We are net importers, and at a strangulation price. Today all the lands and people east of the Ottawa River are dependent on supplies of foreign oil. They are held ransom to fragile supply arrangements from unstable foreign lands, over long water distances and at high world prices. Why? Because governments since the early seventies have not had the foresight or the wisdom to develop western reserves, nor the common sense to build a pipeline past Montreal into Atlantic Canada. Instead, these same governments were content to tax Canadians for social and foreign aid programs we could not afford, while neglecting to finance and assist in the development and transmission of vital energy.
This year, 1980, we will spend $5 billion for foreign oil. That is enough to build a tar sands plant, and every single year until we get down to developing our own reserves adequately we will spend even more. Every year we wait, Atlantic Canada runs the risk of interruption of supply, with terrible conse-

May 8, 1980
Energy Policy
quences to farmers and fishermen, to their factories, and to the heating of their homes. What action do we get to help the citizens of Atlantic Canada? Just the crossing of fingers in the hope that Hibernia will turn out to be the biggest goldarned oil find in the world. We all hope that that will prove to be the case, but that is hardly the stuff of which sound energy policy is made.
How does the government plan to develop Canada's energy? How will it raise the vast sums of money-the hundred plus billion dollars-needed to pay for development of the western oil reserves and the tar sands? Well, it does not know. It does not have a plan. The present government, after joining the NDP to defeat the only plan for energy development Canada has ever had, after only seven months of Conservative government, has come up with no plan, no action, and no pricing formula, unless we take the blended price, which will probably add up to more than our formula.
No one should be surprised that a political party which has its entire power base in eastern Canada finds it impossible to accept the economic realities of the need to pay a higher price for oil. In their blatant grasping for votes they have prujudiced Canada's economic future. No one in Canada wants to pay more for gasoline, and neither do the Americans, the Japanese nor the West Germans, but they do not have a choice, as we do. They have no oil of their own, so they pay world prices, but they have accepted it. They have reacted positively to it, and they have prospered in spite of it. We, who do not have enough oil of our own, pay the world price too for the 20 per cent of our oil which we must import and which is increasing as a percentage due to the increasing annual consumption and the diminishing supply. Unless we undertake a crash program of exploration and development of the tar sands, we will be paying the world price too in this century.
The Conservative energy program, with its 18 cents a gallon and $4 a barrel, was designed to do at least three important things. First, it would keep us from going deeper into debt each year with the Arabs and the Venezuelans. Second, it would have encouraged reductions in consumption of gasoline by encouraging the use of smaller cars, car pools, public transit and any other way one can economize. Third, it would pay for a massive program of energy development, with all its future benefits. How did these farsighted, long-range Liberal planners react to this first ever plan for Canadian energy self-sufficiency? They rejected it. They defeated it. They denied the people of Canada the fantastic benefits of and pride in the achieving not only of energy but also of economic self-sufficiency. They said Canadians could not afford it. They said Canadians could not afford to pay $1.40 a gallon when Americans pay $1.60 and some people over $3.
Does anyone here seriously believe that we are not paying higher prices for gasoline today? Just because the pump price is $1.10 or so, that does not mean we are paying $1.10 a gallon. There are three billion extra dollars which do not appear on the pumps but which must still be paid by all Canadians, whether they drive cars or not, through their taxes to pay the Arabs and the Venezuelans for our shortfall.
History will reveal the cost of Liberal duplicity. Each year we wait will cost Canada billions of wasted dollars.
Instead of saying that we cannot afford higher prices, we should recognize that we cannot afford not to have the benefits which higher prices will bring. Take, for example, my province of Ontario. Ontario produces half of all the manufactures of Canada. How then could Canada spend $100 billion out west without a fantastic boom occurring in Ontario or in Quebec where over half of all the things that go into the building of a high technology industry like the tar sands development originate? If we spend $100 billion in western Canada by 1990, about $25 billion will come back to Ontario and Quebec for the production of pipe, valves, turbines, generators, pumps, trucks, in an industry which desperately needs jobs, computers, building materials, not only for plants but for the thousands of new homes which will go into the new plant sites accompanying the plants, and so on. Who will build these homes and manufacture these goods? Ontario and Quebec companies, and Ontario and Quebec people. In fact companies and people from every province in Canada will benefit from this unprecedented job boom.
Just yesterday Foothills Pipe Lines announced that Stelco in Hamilton and Interprovincial Steel and Pipe Corporation in Regina were given an order for pipe for the Alaska gas pipeline project worth $2 billion. This represents 5,500 man years or person years for Canadians. These companies, working with over 300 suppliers throughout Canada, will provide
28.000	man years of employment. Is anyone so blind that they cannot see the job opportunities, skills, training opportunities and investment opportunities for all Canadians? Even teachers, that hard-hit profession, will be pressed hard to teach the skills which will be in such great demand across Canada.
In the case of the Quebec and maritime pipeline, which would be an investment of over $4 billion, over $3 billion would accrue to Quebec and the maritimes and would create
64.000	man years of jobs over the next two decades. Add to these the jobs, the opportunities for the merchants and businesses along the route and you begin to get an idea of what developing our resources means in terms of jobs and wealth to Canadians. Today a tar sands plant will cost upward of $5 billion. For every plant built, Ontario will benefit to the tune of $ 1 billion.
Another major benefit which would have accrued to Ontario and to all Canadians through the Conservative energy policy, would have been the guaranteed 85 per cent of world price maximum for gasoline and oil, and even less for natural gas, in fact only 72 per cent of world oil price. Compare such benefits for Canadian manufacturing and job-creating opportunities with the speculative purchase of foreign energy supplies which offer no opportunities to Canada. Here we have, on the one hand, tenuous or questionable supply linked to rapidly escalating world price. The spot market oil prices today range in the $40 to $50 a barrel bracket. On the other hand, we could be
May 8, 1980

enjoying guaranteed supply at much lower prices by creating jobs for Canadians. So which is preferable?
Shall we pay fellow Canadians to develop our resources and produce our energy needs from our Canadian companies, or shall we pay foreigners for their oil, make them rich at our expense and enable them to invest our former dollars to buy out Canadian companies? With sound energy policies we could already have been maltres chez nous, masters of our own destiny, instead of potentially shivering in the cold and dependent on foreigners as Liberal government inaction has had us do.
In the debate over increased costs of petroleum energy, Ontario took a firm position against such an increase, largely on the grounds of loss of jobs in Ontario caused by inability to compete due to higher costs. That was the argument. They used the old "we can't afford it" argument. In terms of total energy needs, Ontario today can generate just over 22 per cent of its requirements. It has recognized that through conservation and conversion to indigenous forms of energy, largely electrical, it can supply a target objective of 35 per cent of its total energy requirements by 1995.
Can this be accomplished without cost to the taxpayer? Of course not. The price tag, by the Ontario government's estimate, will be $30 billion over the next 15 years. This huge sum of $30 billion should be recognized as a quarter as much as the entire Conservative government proposal for petroleum selfsufficiency, and yet will supply only a 12 per cent increase in Ontario energy needs. So how can it be justified? Why would a province commit $30 billion for 12 per cent more energy? For benefits, that is how. Ontario sees the benefits of lower cost power and reliability of supply of power. These tangible elements of energy supply will attract and encourage the establishment and development of increased industrial growth, particularly in the high technology industries with increased tax payout and job creation for the province. Ontario also foresees a comcomitant reduction in increasingly expensive petroleum consumption, thus reducing the external influence and the extra costs to its economic affairs.
Now let us look at what Canada's smallest province plans to do about its energy problem. P.E.I. is actively considering the biomass alternative. Its studies show that under today's conditions, for every dollar spent on energy importation, primarily petroleum, 90 cents leave the province. The satisfactory development of biomass would reverse this condition and keep 80 cents of every dollar within the province.
So both the most populous and least populous provinces have recognized the advantage of substantial investment for the long-term benefit of their citizens. Their policies are pay now, benefit later, the very spirit and attitude which built this country. What a contrast this is to the do-nothing, unimaginative, inactive federal Liberal government which seriously jeopardizes Canada's economic future and leaves it under the control of foreigners. Even today it is not too late for the government to realize the error of its ways, to change its direction, to recognize the need to raise oil prices in order to generate the funds needed to commence the huge task before
Energy Policy
us and, at the same time, revitalize the sagging Canadian economy. The world would welcome such a change and would be anxious to participate. Investment dollars would flow into Canada with the consequential rise in the value of the Canadian dollar, the creation of new companies, both within and around the energy field, and the rise in employment which would be immediate and dramatic.
What would be down the road? In a world short of energy, Canada would be unique, a blessed nation, a nation with not only sufficient energy but with a strong industrial base to use that energy, to make productive use of it for the well-being and social benefit of its citizens.
So to the government I say: Please take up the challenge, recognize the potential, take the steps necessary to achieve the vision of a nation which has the resources, has the knowledge, and has the resolve to realize its destiny.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE TO FORMULATE HONEST AND EFFECTIVE ENERGY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate on a motion from the opposition which deplores the absence of an honest and efficient energy policy.
Some hon. members said this afternoon that it takes nerve and temerity to present such a motion at the beginning of this Thirty-second Parliament and I agree. I heard the hon. member who spoke before me say that we have no development policy in the field of energy. I would like to point out to him that our development policy in the field of energy applies to all provinces, not only to one or two, and I am talking more particularly about the western provinces.
Speaking of energy sources development, I would remind the House that during the short time it was in power the previous government, which is the official opposition today, agreed to allow massive exports of natural gas to the United States. That government agreed such exports without any guarantee of any kind as to the construction of a pipeline or as to the possible exchange of gas between the two countries, namely the state of Alaska and Canada. The opposition also made that decision during that short period of time to pave the way for massive exports of one of our most precious natural resources in Canada, a natural resource which among other things is non polluting and one of our most important assets. In doing that, the government of the time had no specific policy or program for Canada in this area, let alone for Canadians. So, Mr. Speaker, it can certainly not be called an efficient policy.
Before the Houses were convened, about a month after the transfer of powers, this government had already accepted and approved a decision by the National Energy Board to start the construction of a Quebec-maritimes gas pipeline, namely the St. Lazare-Boisbriand section, over a distance of some 30 miles. Mr. Speaker, that is what I believe we call efficiency.
870

May 8, 1980
Energy Policy
But we are now faced with another dilemma. After the federal government agreed to have the construction of that section started, we are faced with another government that certainly has no development policy in the energy area. That government, the government of the province of Quebec, which wants to reduce its dependence on oil by 30 per cent by 1990, and its dependence on natural gas by 25 per cent by 1990, that government has not yet given its approval to the construction of that gas pipeline. We know that pipeline would have enabled 83 billion cubic feet of gas to be moved to a new market in Quebec and the maritimes, which is the equivalent of 40,000 barrels of oil a day.
While the government of Quebec refuses to approve that construction, Quebec energy and resources department experts stated before the National Energy Board that if it is to reach its 25 per cent goal by 1990 Quebec needs the construction of a gas pipeline all the way to Quebec City, a low price for ten years for the consumer and the distributor, and a guaranteed supply of gas from western Canada. You see the incoherence of such a government. While some officials of one of their respected departments, a most important department in view of the crisis we are facing in Canada, are asking the National Energy Board to take measures to step up the development and supply of energy in the province of Quebec, there are ministers who are unable to make decisions, which we feel, in view of the current situation, are probably outright political.
In spite of this, the Quebec minister of energy has indicated that Quebec can pay the world price for its natural gas. How do those who favour the thesis put forward by the Quebec government reconcile their irresponsible approach with the serious opportunities for gas development? Would a sovereign and independent Quebec have access to the natural gas from western Canada and enjoy the same favourable conditions as now?
If Quebec were no longer part of Canada, why should it receive preferential treatment over the United States for natural gas prices? The American markets are nearer to the gas fields than Quebec, and the natural gas sold in the United States brings $4.86 per thousand cubic feet to the Canadian producers compared with $1.51 for the gas sold to Quebec. If Quebeckers had to pay the international prices, the natural gas they now use would cost them $550 million. By comparison, they paid $225 million wholesale in 1979, and this represents only 7 per cent of the energy used in Quebec. If we consider a proportion of 25 per cent, which is the objective for 1990, the cost would rise to about $2 billion at the 1980 international prices for gas.
Mr. Speaker, we really must wonder what would happen in such a case to the energy self-sufficiency plans of the Quebec government. However, if we look at the present policy of the Canadian government, we see that we are trying to develop an energy program on a rational basis. As we have underlined and as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has underlined several times, Petro-Canada, this Canadian corporation which we want to maintain and in which we want to invest more money so that it may become one of the highest rated companies in Canada, continues its explorations in eastern Canada and the northern seas.
The discoveries that Petro-Canada has made already and will certainly continue to make in the future will benefit all Canadians, all Quebeckers, and certainly the entire population of eastern Quebec, especially in the lower St. Lawrence and the Gaspe area. We all know to what extent these peripheral areas depend on energy discoveries at the present time, and we also know that Petro-Canada, because of its discoveries and the proximity of the gulf and the ocean, will be able to develop harbours on the north shore, the lower north shore and also in the Gaspe peninsula, and will eventually be able to think about building more plants.
It is extremely important, especially for the population of eastern Quebec, to share fairly in all these Canadian resources and in all this wealth. How can we, in Quebec, accept all that is being said at the present time in our province simply to convince part of the population, a part which I must say is getting smaller and smaller, as we shall certainly be able to see when the next poll is published, which should be tomorrow, I believe. We shall certainly see then that this percentage of the Quebec population is decreasing at a rate that the members of the Parti Quebecois and the Quebec government will certainly find alarming.
Mr. Speaker, I am coming back to the members of the Parti Quebecois who, as I was saying, claim that Hydro-Quebec will provide the money necessary to purchase oil and gas at world prices. This money will be obtained by selling electricity to the United States. The Quebec energy and resources minister said the following to a Radio-Canada reporter on March 10:
We are going to depend increasingly on the international market for our oil; on the other hand, we will have ever larger quantities of electricity which can be seen in the framework of energy exchanges. That is to say, we sell our electricity at a high price and use the profits on that electricity to purchase our oil, so that in fact the cost of energy in Quebec will continue to be very low.
That, Mr. Speaker, is what the Quebec minister of energy spreads around the whole province almost daily. This afternoon, my colleague the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras) quoted figures on oil. He mentioned that the estimates of the Quebec government do not correspond with what this party foresees. Well, just for a few moments, I should like to look at the forecast expansion of the Hydro-Quebec grid. In 1985, the surplus electricity available for export would reach a peak. At that time, Quebec would still be able to pay, with the help of its hydro exports, only 10 per cent of the total cost for oil imports. That, Mr. Speaker, does not take into account the world price it will have to pay for natural gas. As I said earlier, the Quebec government in 1990 wants to have at least 25 per cent of its energy requirements covered by natural gas.
May 8, 1980

In my view, Mr. Speaker, they are somewhat over-confident in their optimism on hydroelectric surpluses. It must be realized that these surpluses are short-term spin-offs. In other words, Mr. Speaker, when new power plants go on stream and provincial demand is lower than production, the surplus is sold in the United States. Current Hydro-Quebec projections are that after 1985 these surpluses will decline significantly. By 1995, provincial demand for hydro power should balance supply.
Even if the total production capacity currently built in the James Bay project were exported at twice today's price, gross revenue would be around $1.7 billion. This would leave no margin for conversion to electricity in Quebec, and leave a $2.6 billion deficit at the 1979 oil costs, and a $5.1 billion one at the current 1980 prices.
This shows that the Quebec government projections for future energy alternatives are totally out of line. They quote figures out of nowhere, they base their assumptions on an expected power yield that is totally unjustified. It is unfortunate in my view that the Quebec government ministers try to convince part of the people with unverified and unverifiable assumptions to document their point on the viability of independence, in a period of energy crisis where we know that the nation's greatest opportunities lie within other provinces. It is unfortunate that they come and tell the people that within 15 years the benefits from hydro power can balance the loss of oil supplies. It is most unfortunate that they use such an issue that is so vitally important to the survival of the people, that they make such points with partisan motives and nothing else.
I feel we should stick to the facts that now exist, and to the Canadian reality. As far as the federal government is concerned, what we want to do, what we want is precisely a development plan, by a corporation like Petro-Canada, which would allow us to divide the existing wealth and by which the province of Quebec, within a united country, could partake of the benefits and of the vast potential that we have. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the people of Quebec, faced with all these facts and vast opportunities, will decide to continue being part of this great country in order to benefit from the policies our government has implemented, the policies it is implementing and also from everything the government intends to do in this regard so that the province of Quebec and the maritimes will have maximum benefit.
Mr. Speaker, as I have tried to show, all the Quebec government is trying to make us believe is that the demand for electricity will allow it to make up its deficit, especially its monetary deficit, so that Quebec can get its oil supply. But again, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that we can believe those statements, and that is why our government, as the minister stated this afternoon, intends to take action in the field of energy so that all of Canada can satisfy all its energy needs.
Energy Policy

I see that there is now half a minister in the House. We do not know what he does to earn his salary, but the half of him is here.
The deficit in that last year of office was increased by $2 billion to pay for imported oil. This is that same old government which fought an election and won it on the issue of preventing an 18-cent a gallon increase and is now faced with the necessity of imposing a 16-cent a gallon increase almost immediately, with much more to come later, and that cannot be denied.

speechtext:
Nowhere have the weakness and evasiveness of the government been more evident than on the question of energy pricing. They know full well they cannot go on subsidizing oil imports at the expense of the taxpayer, piling up huge and dangerous deficits. The cost of financing this government's deficits is now a major component of our annual expenditures. Our government tried to face up to this situation. It was an element of the budget introduced by the hon. member for St. John's West. Yet this vacillating government continues to pretend that it is offering Canadians cheap, or relatively cheap gas, and in that very fact encourages waste.
If one were to talk about their so-called policies on conservation, there has been no attempt whatsoever at providing leadership in the field of energy conservation by the government. Quite to the contrary. One simple way in which oil conservation could be encouraged, would be a reduction in the price of natural gas which would give Canadians an incentive to convert from oil to natural gas. Another example of this government's erratic energy posture was the meeting between the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and Premier Bennett of British
May 8, 1980

Columbia just a day or two ago, the details of which still remain shrouded in mystery.
It is, however, authoritatively reported that the Prime Minister offered to provide federal funding for the proposed B.C.-Japanese coal project only on the condition that B.C. would make some kind of tax concessions for the Alaska highway natural gas pipeline. If there has been a more blatant betrayal of the pipeline project, I do not know where it is recorded. The supreme irony is that this comes from the Prime Minister- who has been accusing the Clark government of fumbling this very pipeline, an accusation which he knew to be false when he made it.
When the Prime Minister goes to work, he does not fumble, he simply knifes the project in the back and does it behind closed doors. I cannot say that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is very far behind him in the manner in which he has been manipulating, or attempting to manipulate, the decisions of the National Energy Board, which is supposed to be a free and independent agency of the government, making its own free and independent decisions.
The latest episode in the oil pricing charade is when the federal Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources issues provocative statements such as the one he made to the Conference Board yesterday, to the effect that Alberta, and I am quoting him, "cannot use its resources to the detriment of the rest of Canada." He said that again today. While he was saying it, it took me back to the days when I lived in the maritime provinces. The people down there felt very deprived. They felt that eastern Canada was lying under the udder of the cow; the front end of the cow was feeding the prairie provinces, and guess what the maritimes got? That is what they are getting under this government as well.
What does that mean, Mr. Speaker? Does the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources make that kind of statement about Saskatchewan selling its potash at world prices, or does it mean that Quebec is marketing its hydro power-does he make the statement with respect to that matter-or Ontario its wood pulp or gold-does he mean it should sell its nickel at world prices as he insists that Alberta does with its resources, and Saskatchewan too?
It is a dangerous game that is being played by the Liberal party and the Liberal government, both in Alberta and British Columbia. I might say that this does nothing at all to encourage unity in this country. The government is playing fast and loose with provincial resources and provincial rights as though these things were within the jurisdiction of the federal bureaucracy. They are not, and the attitude that they are is one of the reasons why we have creeping separatism across this country today. They are deliberately fueling that emotion in this country. There is no question about it. As my friend says, they set about destroying it and they are achieving it in a very admirable fashion, as we see across our northern provincial boundary today. It is a very dangerous game they are playing. There is no question in my mind that if more attention had
Energy Policy
been paid to the rights and needs of the provinces in energy and other fields, we would not be having a referendum in Quebec today.

speechtext:
Federal government spokesmen have been using the same tactic in Quebec as they used in the rest of Canada during the election. They have made energy a political football. They have been going into Quebec and promising cheap oil as an incentive to vote in a certain way in the referendum. Like thousands of others, I hope that Quebec citizens will see where their interests lie and reject the ghetto mentality of the Parti Quebecois and its supporters. But I deplore a tactic which promises what is not theirs to deliver, just as they did during the election campaign last May. The energy crisis in this country will not be resolved as long as this government treats it as political bait, provides no leadership in conservation, and refuses to take the necessary measures to control this situation. The situation in Quebec cannot be resolved on a promise to deliver cheap oil. That is not going to happen.
Energy is a symptom of this government's breakdown in the field of federal-provincial relations, as is their absolute disregard for the constitutional rights of the provinces in every field, including offshore rights about which they continue to make threatening statements. That is why Canada is fragmented and that is why we have a situation in Quebec which is a reflection of a similar uneasiness, felt but not voiced as loudly yet in other provinces.
Recently the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), that jolly jumper, that jovial gentleman who at one stroke rid himself of all contenders for the leadership of his party and returned to office as a part-time Prime Minister, told Canadians-a so-called part-time Prime Minister-that they could easily afford to pay exorbitant interest rates. To young married couples across this country, newly established in expensive homes and following extremely tight budgets, this arrogant bachelor over there says, "pay up or ship out." "You can afford it," he told them from the eminence of his minister's salary, "It is no problem. All my friends," he says, "are in a position to pay." That is an astonishing statement from one who, in earlier years, when the mantle of humility sat on his shoulders at one time, was a paragon of socialist virtues-a man moved to tears in this House by the simple contemplation of the number of Canadians living below the subsistence level.
As if that were not enough, sir, a few days ago he complained in the House-at least I thought he was complaining though he may well have been boasting-that a number of his cabinet colleagues were coming in with expensive programs which might have the effect of increasing the present astronomical deficit even further. There seems to be continuing contention between himself and the minister responsible for DREE.
It is a new and welcome departure to see the minister in the role of watchdog of the public purse. It is unfortunate that he did not adopt that role somewhat sooner, a few years ago, for

May 8, 1980
Energy Policy
example, when his colleagues took their first faltering steps toward the fiscal chasm on which they are now hovering.
Unless they change their ways, Mr. Speaker, and face up to the problems as did the hon. member for St. John's West in his budget of last December, the Apocalypse will be upon us.
