FINANCE-AID TO SYDNEY STEEL AND MICHELIN TIRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, about three weeks ago I asked the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) about the situation with regard to two very important projects to the economy of Nova Scotia, namely, Michelin Tire expansion, and aid to Sysco. I see my friend, the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan) is here in the chamber tonight and I see that he shares my concern although he has been strangely quiet about expressing the same kind of concern that he did when he sat on this side of the House, but I guess that is understandable.
The Minister of Finance sat mute in his seat and permitted the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Harquail) to assure the House that there would be an announcement made very shortly. Enough time has elapsed, about three weeks, that I feel compelled to underscore, once again, the importance of this particular situation not only to the province of Nova Scotia but to the Canadian economy.
I want to take this opportunity also to express my confidence in and my admiration for the new Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. De Bane), a man of sensitivity and a man who, I truly believe, has the interests of all parts of Canada foremost in his mind. As I say, I want to take this first
Adjournment Debate
opportunity to assure him of my good will and support in this regard.
Unfortunately, 1 cannot express the same admirable sentiments when it comes to the attitude and the past record of the Minister of Finance who has had, for a period of ten years, the opportunity as a member of the government of this country, and as a minister from Nova Scotia, to do something. Instead of that he and the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Regan), the former premier of Nova Scotia for nearly a decade, were not part of the solution, they were part of the problem.
However, dealing first with Michelin, may I just put on the record that this is a very important project. To all intents and purposes it was a fait accompli early last winter. There really has been no valid reason for the delay in the confirmation of this very important project which not only will assure that Nova Scotia will be pre-eminent in the field of radial tire technology but, indeed, will ensure a vital stake for Canada in this particularly important industry. The fact that certain parts of Ontario are having difficulty with their segment of the rubber industry certainly should be no reason for anyone to try to deny the obvious merit of proceeding with the Michelin expansion in Nova Scotia. This company makes one of the finest, if not the finest, tires in the world, has fulfilled all of its commitments and should certainly, as a matter of right, be allowed to proceed with an RD1A grant which is not only perfectly in order but which should have been announced weeks ago.
If the government does not wish to proceed on that basis it could certainly proceed under the aegis of a subagreement under the general development agreement between the province and the Government of Canada. So I can only reiterate my hope that the government will get on with this job and stop the delay which is only costing employment and economic impetus to the province of Nova Scotia.
Mr. Speaker, dealing with the Sysco situation, this again is vital to the Nova Scotia economy. On its success rests not only the economic well-being of Cape Breton Island but also the viability of a large industry in Trenton, Nova Scotia, employing some 2,000 people. The Minister of Finance, as a Cape Bretoner, ought to know that delay is the deadliest form of denial. He participated in this tactic for, as I say, almost a decade together with Tom Kent who was probably the most incompetent manager that any large corporation ever had, setting the cause of Sysco back for a decade instead of modernizing and building upon the foundation which existed in 1970 when the government of Nova Scotia had previously, for various reasons, to take over this corporation and which was then producing about a million tons of steel every year under the same chief executive officer who has now come back to try to resuscitate it after ten years of neglect. Instead of doing something at that time, the government continued to obfuscate and delay. Mr. Speaker, there is ample precedent for the Government of Canada doing something immediately to take this economic burden off the province of Nova Scotia. We

May 8, 1980
Adjournment Debate
have the St. Lawrence Seaway reorganization and consolidation of debt; we have the Air Canada situation where a similar burden was lifted, and Nova Scotia deserves at least the kind of economic consideration that wealthier parts of this country have enjoyed from this government.
I see my time has almost elapsed in this brief adjournment debate. May I simply say to the government opposite: Get on with the job. Our government was doing something about it. The government had ten years to do something about it, and since taking office again it looks as if we are back to the same old empty promises exemplified by the grandiose Gabarouse project that the Deputy Prime Minister ate off for years with no results for anyone.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State, Small Businesses):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: FINANCE-AID TO SYDNEY STEEL AND MICHELIN TIRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the present government shares the concern of the hon. member in respect of the future of the Sydney Steel Corporation in Cape Breton and the possibility of additional manufacturing and related activity in Nova Scotia by Michelin Tires (Canada) Limited.
The hon. member is well aware that this government wrote the first significant subsidiary agreement for assistance to the Sydney Steel Corporation in December of 1977, with total commitments close to $20 million. Further significant federal commitment to the Sydney Steel Corporation was made in April, 1979, but was not acted upon by either the province of Nova Scotia or the Government of Canada which assumed power after May 22, 1979. Since that time the circumstances which led to the federal commitment to Sysco have changed considerably. The company and the province decided not to enter into a long-term billets contract with Tree Island Steel Company of British Columbia, and the government of Nova Scotia primarily withdrew from further consideration of comprehensive joint studies which had been made to examine viable future options for the company. 1 am, however, optimistic that Canada and Nova Scotia will resume serious examination of viable future long-term solutions for Sysco.
I have to remind the hon. member, of course, that the Sydney Steel Corporation is a provincial Crown corporation and that decisions as to the future of the corporation are in large part dictated by the objectives of the government of Nova Scotia. 1 can say, however, that I do not believe that short-term remedies for Sysco which have been proposed from time to time constitute the right way to go about solving the problems of the company.
I understand that the province of Nova Scotia presented a proposal to the previous administration in January of this year. No action was taken at that time. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has indicated to the House, he has discussed the Sysco situation with Premier Buchanan at a meeting on April 11 in Halifax and in other telephone conversations. He has also indicated to the House today that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. De Bane) and other members of the government are prepared to sit down with the government of Nova Scotia at any time to consider
concrete plans which will have some prospect of ensuring a viable future for the provincially-owned steel plant at Sydney. He emphasized that any federal contribution will need to be placed in the context of a plan that is based on a viable production, sales and marketing program which can also provide an assurance of the longer term future of Sysco.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: ENERGY-PROTECTION OF LOWER-INCOME GROUPS FROM SEVERE PRICE INCREASES
ENERGY-PROTECTION OF LOWER-INCOME GROUPS FROM SEVERE PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are now at a critical stage in the history of the maritime provinces. New Brunswick, for example, faces grave threats to its economic and social well-being and also significant opportunities to escape some of its chronic difficulties. In 1979-80 it achieved the dubious distinction of having half its provincial revenues derived from Ottawa-a landmark of dependency already passed by Prince Edward Island and soon to be reached by Nova Scotia. Moreover, rising energy costs threaten New Brunswick's single most important industry, the forestry sector, for its mills are substantially more energy-intensive than competitors elsewhere; this at a time when disease control and plant modernization are also urgent. Because social benefits reversed the net migration out of New Brunswick during the 1970s-a good thing in itself-the province has a high unemployment rate despite a respectable record of job creation.
In fact New Brunswick is just now experiencing what most other provinces began adjusting to some time ago-an increasing number of job seekers, especially women, with high educational qualifications and career aspirations to match.
There is one other major obstacle to maritime economic recovery which has been part of our condition for so long we have almost stopped treating it as a problem. If New Brunswick is to have significant manufacturing beyond the processing of its own most skilled and enterprising citizens, then it must identify and develop external markets, and it must have technologies suited to local circumstances. But large companies based outside the region have little reason to invest in such marketing or research and development, and most local companies can seldom afford it.
Those opportunities which must be seized relate mostly to energy. In terms of supply, there are several possibilities for reversing our growing and dangerous reliance on imported oil-dangerous for all of Canada because the country is already subsidizing New Brunswick alone to the tune of about $1 million a day. For Atlantic Canada as a whole, the figure is now well over $3 million.
Expanded hydroelectric capacity, including the harnassing of Fundy tidal power, is the most attractive source because such energy will never run out. We hear mutterings about the prohibitive cost of Fundy power but, as the cost of fossil fuels skyrockets and as we compare estimates for this kind of development with the projected investment in tar sands projects, we are entitled to wonder why the investigation of Fundy has been so slow.
May 8, 1980

We should also be thinking of a regional power grid and drawing on plentiful, distant sources, such as the still underdeveloped potential of the lower Churchill Falls in Labrador. New Brunswick's commitment to nuclear energy has been made in the form of Point Lepreau, which will begin to provide from 20 per cent to 30 per cent of provincial electric requirements next year. The ideal solution for pulp and paper mills is, of course, to convert wood residue to useful energy. Apart from the saving in imported oil, this would be a stimulus for new forest management techniques on both farmlands and private woodlots. Coal and thermal peat have technological obstacles to be overcome, but these resources also exist in abundance.
The question of natural gas is a distinctly two-sided one. There are enormous potential gains for New Brunswick. The Petro-Canada proposal to ship liquefied natural gas from the Arctic to an east coast port, where it would be gasified and piped to central Canadian markets, as well as the more immediate Q and M and TransCanada proposals to ship western gas eastward until Arctic resources are available-all these would command substantial activity. Q and M alone forecasts 5,500 man years over a three-year period.
The availability of natural gas opens up numerous industrial possibilities, including materials for the conversion of users to gas from other forms of energy, plastic pipe for the transmission of gas, and the production of New Brunswick's newly exploited potash resources.
The greatest opportunity of all, however, is for the expansion of Saint John's shipbuilding facilities in order to build liquid natural gas carriers. Experts are agreed that if a proposed two-phase, $50-million program to lengthen and widen the inner dry dock goes ahead, the port's permanent ice-free condition and other modern facilities will make it a strong competitor for vessel contracts.
The danger in natural gas development is long term and controllable, but only if we keep sight of it amidst the present enthusiasm. Gas is a non-renewable resource; the maritimes must learn from their mistake with oil and not become heavily dependent on another vanishing commodity. Natural gas consumption must be treated primarily as a transitional phase, with conservation and non-depleting forms of energy as the ultimate answers.
The previous government demonstrated, in the short time allowed it by the Liberals and their western surrogates, that it understood the problems and the need for immediate, comprehensive action.
Virtually every reputable economic authority in and outside the country, not to mention previous Liberal ministers of finance and energy, recognized that there could be no successful conservation campaign and no adequate development of alternate energy sources, until oil prices began rising toward realistic levels. The proposed energy bank was precisely the kind of mechanism through which research and conversion could be financed in the maritimes, and it would have provided
Adjournment Debate
the impetus, finally, to activate the Maritime Energy Corporation as the basis for a co-ordinated, long-term regional strategy. The budget also recognized the need to cushion the impact of oil price increases during the period of transition, hence both the shelter allowance and the subsidy for oil-generated electricity.
For an average maritime family of four driving 12,000 miles a year, getting 20 miles per gallon for gas and earning under $21,000 a year, the energy tax credit of $80 per adult and $30 per child would have amounted to $220-and fully compensated for the 18-cent excise increase and $4 a barrel price increase. Whatever the government's eventual position on oil pricing, I recommend that special consideration like this be given Canadians in the lower and middle income brackets, and that a goal of energy self-sufficiency stress development of our indigenous energy sources.

speakeroldname: Mr. Russell MacLellan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State, Mines):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: ENERGY-PROTECTION OF LOWER-INCOME GROUPS FROM SEVERE PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the minister responded to the questions from the hon. member for York Sunbury (Mr. Howie), he explained that he was in the process of negotiating with the producing provinces on oil prices and, until that process was completed, he would not know the extent to which the new price structure might impose a burden on the Atlantic provinces. It could be said with certainty, however, that the impact of a price increase would have been much greater under the planned budget of the previous government. In fact, the price increase this year will be less than half of what it would have been under the Tories.
The government is examining Atlantic provinces needs in the context of the over-all energy strategy now being developed. Specific programs can only be worked out, however, when revenues that will be available to the federal government are known, and this information must await a determination of oil price conditions. The very considerable assistance that has been provided to the Atlantic provinces in relation to oil costs should not be forgotten.
Over the years the federal government has provided assistance in a variety of ways to assist the maritime provinces in meeting their electricity requirements. The assistance dates from the early 1960s when funds were provided under the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act. More recently support has been provided through federal loans to aid New Brunswick in construction of the Point Lepreau nuclear generating station, and Nova Scotia through funds to advance construction on the second coal-fired thermal generating unit at the Lingan coal mine. Prince Edward Island has been assisted through the construction of the interconnecting cable providing lower cost electrical energy from its neighbouring provinces. Assistance to Newfoundland is being provided through the Lower Churchill Development Corporation leading to proposals for hydroelectric development in Labrador and related electrical transmissions systems.
The federal government is strongly committed to the Maritime Energy Corporation as a means of achieving a co-opera-

May 8, 1980
Adjournment Debate
tive effort in the planning and development of efficient electrical distribution throughout the maritime provinces. The federal government stands ready to provide financial support to this broader degree of regional co-operation and planning as soon as the maritime provinces reach a consensus on a procedure that would permit the necessary co-ordination. Any further studies of the Bay of Fundy tidal power must await the establishment of the Maritime Energy Corporation in accordance with a memorandum of understanding signed by the three maritime governments and the federal government in February, 1979.
1 should like to remind hon. members of the huge amount of assistance that has been provided to residents of the Atlantic provinces, in respect of oil price increases, by way of the oil import compensation program. During the past six years the people of the Atlantic provinces have benefited from this program to the extent of about $2.5 billion, or approximately $1,100 per person over a six-year period.

ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-ALLEGED ILLEGALITIES COMMITTED BY MEMBERS OF FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise this evening to raise some very serious questions concerning the RCMP operation Checkmate, the McDonald commission, and the role of the Liberal government to date in these matters. I might add that unfortunately the Conservative party in this Parliament has been totally silent, both inside and outside the House, on these important points concerning the responsibilities of the government to uphold the rule of law in this country.
Operation Checkmate, which was disclosed on April 19 and 20, made reference to a number of illegal operations carried out under the guise of disruptive measures pursuant to the alleged mandate of the RCMP security service. The concern that I have on this question is that if we are to respect the principle that there cannot be one law for the RCMP and another law for the rest of Canadians-and surely this must be a cardinal principle under our system of law in this country- where there is clear evidence of wrongdoing, either criminal wrongdoing or under another federal statute, it is incumbent upon the government to prosecute that wrongdoing.
Of course, we have seen where there are prosecutions in some cases that the courts will consider the circumstances in arriving at a sentence, such as in the case of Superintendent Cobb who was given an absolute discharge in connection with the APLQ break-in. Unfortunately, the attitude of this government, however, appears to be not one of upholding the concept of the rule of law, but rather saying that if certain actions to date on the part of the RCMP have been illegal, if the RCMP have been breaking the law, then we must change the law. That appears to be the concept of the Liberal government, and that is a concept which we on this side of the House reject.
I would point only to the example of mail opening. We have seen a succession of evidence of illegal mail opening, many instances of mail opening, and the response of the government. The hasty response of the new Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) has been: well, perhaps what we should be doing, then, is changing the law to make this very serious invasion of our privacy legal. Once again, we reject that response to this question.
There are a number of remedies which the government can consider in dealing with violations of the law by the RCMP. Basically there are three such remedies. First, there is a question of prosecution either by provincial attorneys general or by the federal attorney general. Of course, the question of jurisdiction was one of the questions which arose in my exchange with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on April 21.
It is clearly beyond any doubt under criminal law in this country that the federal government has the responsibility and, indeed, the exclusive jurisdiction to prosecute under federal statutes such as the Post Office Act or the Income Tax Act. Indeed, the Supreme Court of Canada has left open the question as to whether the federal government has jurisdiction to prosecute under the Criminal Code of Canada, that is, of course, in the Hauser decision of the Supreme Court of Canada. Prosecution is one remedy that is available.
A second remedy is disciplinary proceedings against those members of the RCMP who have been found to have violated the law, and thirdly there is the question of civil action by those persons or groups who have been aggrieved by the illegal actions of the RCMP. This is a time-consuming and expensive method of proceeding on these wrongdoings, however.
The significant factor in all of these cases of wrongdoing today is that there has not been a single charge, not a single prosecution in respect of any of these wrongdoings. It is that fact which is causing very serious questions to arise in the minds of Canadians as to the desire of this government and its predecessor to uphold the rule of law in this country.
We have seen a series of offences under the Criminal Code; forgery, breaking and entering, theft and impersonation. 1 suggest it is encumbent upon this government not to hide behind the smokescreen of the McDonald commission, but to proceed to show Canadians that where the law is violated there is a responsibility on the part of the government to prosecute under that law, and that there is one law for all Canadians.
We in the New Democratic Party expressed serious concern at the time of the formation of the McDonald commission, in a number of areas, including the limited terms of reference of this commission and its failure to have any mandate to look at the question of political accountability of the security service. We were frankly concerned about the political background of a number of the commissioners and, indeed, of some of the senior staff, and that was a background of active involvement in the Liberal party.
We are concerned that the RCMP must not be allowed to be made scapegoats if the responsibility for their illegal actions
May 8, 1980

lies higher up in the political chain. The commission has been going for approximately three years, and at every instance when the illegal actions of the RCMP have been disclosed we have been told by members of the government that we will have to await the outcome of that commission.
We say that the time has come to act. The Prime Minister has indicated that he intends to await the outcome of the commission report. We say, based on the record of the commission so far, and based particularly on the record of the commission in its first report on the Official Secrets Act, that we have very little cause for optimism, indeed, that this report will not be satisfactory to deal with the concerns we have in this area.
In closing I would like to say that there are two major points on which we would like some clarification. The first is, are the disruptive measures which were used by the RCMP in operation Checkmate still authorized under the mandate of the security service today, and are they being carried out? Secondly, as I asked the Prime Minister, what happened to the files which were destroyed pertaining to operation Checkmate, and who authorized that destruction?
There are many other serious questions in this area of the RCMP and the law, and I am sure that in the days ahead they will be raised.

speakeroldname: Mr. Russell MacLellan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State, Mines):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-ALLEGED ILLEGALITIES COMMITTED BY MEMBERS OF FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as both the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) have stated, it is not the policy of the government to comment on the day to day proceedings of the commission of inquiry. This includes the details of operation Checkmate and the destruction of associated files, which matter is also under investigation by the commission.
It can be said, however, that it is the Solicitor General's policy, as it has been of his immediate predecessors, to direct the framework of the law. As for the future, the government is considering future arrangements to govern the activities of the
Adjournment Debate
RCMP, and in this regard the government hopes that the forthcoming report of the commission of inquiry will be useful.
The laying of charges is not the responsibility of the Prime Minister or the Solicitor General, but a unique prerogative of the attorneys general, federal and provincial, depending on the nature of the case. However, Mr. Justice McDonald has clearly indicated that he would prefer any such action to await his report, and in view of the fact that he is committed to report during the summer it seems reasonable to give the commission this opportunity.
The government recognizes that the provincial attorneys general are fully responsible to determine what action they should take and when it should be taken. The Solicitor General has offered consultations to them, and two provincial attorneys general have taken up his offer, as a result of which further information under his control will be provided to them. In the event, however, that any of the attorneys general seek access to the in-camera transcripts of the proceedings of the commission, it should be borne in mind that the commissioners have taken position that the control of such material is theirs exclusively. Accordingly, in such circumstances it would be necessary for the Solicitor General to discuss any such requests with the commissioners.
The commission itself established rules that determine who is authorized to have access to the transcripts of its in-camera proceedings. The Government of Canada has access to such transcripts, but for it to circulate the information further would in the view of the commissioners, be contrary to the rules of the commission, If, however, any of the attorneys general involved decide to make formal representations to the Solicitor General to secure access to the in-camera transcripts, the Solicitor General is prepared to discuss the matter further with the commission.
